en: The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Four Youthful Disciples,
Volume One. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of Gandhāra in North India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the country of Kuśinagara, at the site of the Mallas, between two twin śāla trees in the Śāla Grove.
At that time, the Tathāgata reflected:
"Today the time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived; I should now enter extinction.

That very night, the Elder Ānanda suddenly had a nightmare; filled with terror, anxiety, and distress, he hurried to the Buddha’s presence, and with a sorrowful countenance and palms joined, he gazed up at the World-Honored One, his eyes never wavering for a moment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Ānanda:
"Son of Gautamī! Why do you gaze at me so intently, your eyes not blinking for even a moment?"
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Last night I suddenly saw a dream; my body hair stood on end and I was filled with great terror. This must surely be a precursor to the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa."
“World-Honored One!
Having seen these inauspicious dreams, my heart finds no peace; I am deeply distressed and filled with anxiety, fearing that the World-Honored One will swiftly enter parinirvāṇa.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Son of Gautamī! What dream did you see that made you know it to be a precursor to the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, causing you to give rise to such alarm and fear?"
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed Ānanda with these verses:
"What did you see in your dream, in the Śāla grove,
which was said to be a precursor to nirvāṇa?"
"Please explain those signs to me.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
"The dream I saw last night was terrifying, causing the hair on my body to stand on end."
Filled with great alarm and trepidation, we pray that the World-Honored One will now grant us his attention.
Suddenly, within this world, there has appeared a vast tree,
exquisite and most beautiful to behold, always bearing flowers and fruit.
Universally covering the realm of sentient beings, its shade is most refreshing and cool.
If one takes refuge beneath this tree, one receives joy and is freed from sorrow and affliction;
by beholding the tree, one attains the pure eye, and by hearing its sound, one attains the pure ear.
Having accomplished manifold merits, it rises as high as the Peak of Existence.
From that tree issues a wondrous sound, fully explaining the characteristics of all phenomena;
complete with subtle and profound meanings, it brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
Those trees emit radiance, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
filling such realms; there is nowhere it does not pervade throughout all the worlds of the ten directions— immeasurable and inconceivable.
Those touched by its radiance shall surely obtain benefit;
that tree emits a wondrous fragrance, universally perfuming the lands of the ten directions.
If one smells this fragrance, they shall not fall into the various evil realms.
They shall not fall into hell, nor into the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, or asuras; they shall all reach the happy destinies.
Such a great and wondrous tree brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
Having crushed the ground of the Mallas, he lay between the twin trees. At that time,
a multitude numbering in the thousands— immeasurable and inconceivable—
seeing this great tree fall, wailed and wept in sorrow.
Suddenly I no longer heard that sound, nor did I smell any fragrance;
each was unable to rise of their own accord, and I too fell down in a state of bewildered distress.
Such were my dreams yesterday—countless signs of terror.
"Tell me, who possesses the eye of wisdom, of the matters as I have seen them.

At that time, the various devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, Brahmā Sahāmpati, lord of the Sahā world, together with Māra the Prince, Lord of Merchants; Śakra Devendra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and their respective retinues—each having heard from their own abodes of the signs of the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the World-Honored One—along with more than eighty nayutas of devaputras in their retinues, surrounded him from front and back, proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and all with one voice wailed in grief and distress, weeping with sorrowful tears.
He then addressed Ānanda with these verses:
"Alas, what great suffering!
Ānanda, you who possess full knowledge, The Tathāgata, between the twin śāla trees, Intends to enter parinirvāṇa."
"For those without a lamp, you have become a lamp; for those without refuge, you have become a refuge.
Desiring to enter into tranquility, [you shall attain] the great nirvana without remainder.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to the Venerable Ānanda and the assembly of devas:
“O virtuous one, do not grieve; it is exactly as you have seen.
This very night, he will enter parinirvāṇa beneath the twin śāla trees.
Those great trees possess branches and trunks of inconceivable wonder.”
Possessing radiant fragrance, he has been crushed between the twin trees.
As with the tree, so it is with the Buddha; now I wish to go to that place where he enters parinirvāṇa without remainder, like water extinguishing a great fire.
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others—those foremost in supernormal powers and wisdom—have already entered parinirvāṇa; do you not know this now?
All conditioned phenomena are thus: they are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing.
The Buddha knows these characteristics; having known them, he teaches them to the multitude. Ānanda!
You should inform my śrāvakas: the Elder Nandika, foremost in the divine eye;
the Elder Kātyāyana, the Elder Kauṣṭhila, Pūrṇa, Subhūti, Nanda, and Gavāmpati.
King Śūṇamoka, those who wear rag-robes, Nanda and Rāhula, as well as the other śrāvakas—
both those in training and those beyond training— and all other ordinary worldlings.
Inform everyone quickly; before long I shall pass into parinirvāṇa.
Do not give rise to such suffering after my nirvāṇa.
Both those in training and ordinary worldlings suffer greatly when they do not see me.
"I comforted them and explained the true nature of phenomena:
'All conditioned things are like dreams; they are impermanent, so do not grieve.
When the World-Honored One had spoken thus, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
“World-Honored One!
Hearing that the Buddha intends to enter parinirvāṇa, my grief and anxiety are no small matter;
my body is stricken with fear and devoid of joy, while my heart’s sorrow and lamentation increase all the more.”
Detachment from desire is likewise so: how does that eye depart?
How did you inform the Elder, the foremost of all eyes, that today the Greatly Compassionate Honored One, having been seen, shall not be seen again?
I am now personally afflicted by suffering; how can I tell them of their own suffering?
Elder, having heard of such matters of great distress and terror, how should those in training and other ordinary worldlings abide?
Pierced by the arrows of sorrow and grief, I pray that the World-Honored One remain for an eon.
How can you proclaim to the fourfold assembly that the World-Honored One has passed into extinction?
May the World-Honored One explain this to me; I pray that the World-Honored One remain for an eon.
The great torch has passed away with swift speed; it has vanished from the world.
There will be great darkness in the world, and the world will be forever blind.
I am unable to inform them of this great suffering that has befallen the world.
"The World-Honored One has sent others instead—those who have no sorrow or suffering.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Son of Gautamī!"
"Do not grieve or suffer; the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "Ānanda!..."
Hundreds of millions of devas, hearing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, all abandoned their celestial palaces, overcome with grief and great anguish.
Attendant, you who are of right conduct, go and inform the bhikṣus:
"After my parinirvāṇa, they will suffer in distress at no longer seeing me."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was preaching the Dharma for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven atop Mount Sumeru.

Then, with his purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, he saw the sons of the gods of great majesty and virtue abandoning their palaces; he further heard the gods crying out, wailing, and weeping in loud lamentation, and he saw his own followers and retinue all dispersing in every direction.

At that time, Aniruddha, with profound mindfulness and the clarity of his divine eye, observed again and again how the various devaputras and their retinues, abandoning their own sensual pleasures, were filled with sorrow, grief, and distress as they swiftly departed one after another.

At that time, Aniruddha further beheld Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and its various peaks—some a hundred yojanas high, some two hundred, three hundred, or four hundred yojanas—which were being stripped away, split apart, and toppled over; or five hundred yojanas, or even immeasurable Sumeru peaks, collapsing and falling into the great ocean waters, yet without causing any affliction or harm to the sentient beings therein.
He does not even harm or afflict a single sentient being, much less many;
nor does he injure a single sentient being, much less when it comes to injuring many.

All the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas who dwell upon that king of mountains, Sumeru, hearing that the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, were all filled with grief and sorrow, giving rise to great anguish; they simultaneously set out for the city of Kuśinagara, traveling with swift and urgent haste.
At that moment, the peaks of Mount Sumeru suddenly collapsed and the earth shook with a great roar, as voices cried out:

"Now the Great Śākya, Śākyamuni, the supreme king among the Śākyas, who has practiced various roots of goodness through asceticism for incalculable billions of kalpas, desires now to enter the nirvāṇa of unconditioned extinction between the twin śāla trees in the Śāla grove at the birthplace of the Mallas."
"All the devas and humans shall surely perish before our eyes.
They all became frantic and hurried along, causing Mount Sumeru and the great waters of the ocean to tremble and shake.
Because of this event, the peaks of this great king of mountains, Sumeru, and its great mountain valleys collapsed and fell, sinking into the great ocean.
At that time, Aniruddha, who was staying atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, immediately let out a loud voice and spoke these verses:
"The Great Caravan Leader of the world, The Great Field of Merit for all sentient beings,"
Having bestowed the rewards of worldly happiness, this seer now enters nirvana.
In the past he was able to perform great meritorious deeds; as a great king of physicians, he treated all ailments.
He extracted thorns with unimpeded ease and remained free from attachment; that seer now desires to enter nirvana.
Seeing that sentient beings are afflicted by many desires, revolving through ignorance, birth, and old age and death,
and dwelling in the prison of inverted views, he gives rise to great compassion and preaches the Dharma for them.
When the hosts of Māras stir up anger and come forth, Wielding fierce blades with intent to cause harm,
Or grasping great boulders and mountain precipices, Displaying all manner of terrifying sights—
Though such multitudes are most fearsome, Upon seeing them, his body hairs do not tremble.
That Honored One, who was able to destroy such Māras, now desires to enter parinirvāṇa between the twin trees.
Stretching forth his right hand and pointing it toward the earth, he makes the villages and all the mountains tremble and roar.
That Seer, the Sovereign Great Dharma King, now desires to attain nirvāṇa within the twin grove.
He can strike the great earth and produce a mighty sound that is heard throughout the inconceivable worlds of the ten directions;
that supreme being of great wisdom now desires to enter nirvana between the twin śāla trees.
In the past, when the hosts of Māra were most terrifying, he had already attained the state of fearlessness that is unshakable.
That Great Sage preached for the multitude, turning the great Dharma-wheel of the Four Truths;
manifesting spiritual powers beyond compare, he placed all worlds upon the tip of a single hair.
Sentient beings do not know, nor do they perceive, That the Honored One now intends to enter nirvāṇa.
Having now reached the site of the Mallas, Amidst the twin śāla trees,
He has entered the samādhi of great tranquility, About to proceed toward nirvāṇa like the extinguishing of a fire.

At that time, after the Venerable Aniruddha had spoken these verses, by the supernatural power of the Buddha, all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās within Jambudvīpa—excluding the Elder Mahākāśyapa and his circle of disciples and followers—namely the remaining assembly of two hundred and four bhikṣus and all other members of the fourfold assembly, rushed toward the grove of the twin śāla trees. They gathered together and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, each thinking:
"This is now our final opportunity to behold the World-Honored One."

When Aniruddha had spoken this verse, at that very moment, all the gods and celestial beings of great majesty throughout the trichiliocosm—including the sons and daughters of the gods, the nāgas, nāga sons, and nāga daughters; the yakṣas, yakṣa males and females; the piśācas, piśāca males and females; and all the devas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and those who dwell among the constellations—[were moved].

Thus, this entire great assembly all wailed and wept; blood flowed, drenching the ground, their faces covered with tears and their eyes filled with sorrow. Their hearts were clouded by grief, and they raised their voices in cries, wailing and roaring in such lamentation that heaven and earth were shaken.

Pierced by the arrow of sorrow, his heart was devoid of reliance; he lamented and sighed with deep grief, uttering moans and groans. His faculties were stifled by despair, and he suddenly fell into a state of fainting and collapse. Rolling upon the ground, his entire body trembled violently as his hands and feet dangled, enduring great anguish and distress.
Among them, some looked at one another and wept;
some struck their own heads with their fists and lacerated their faces and bodies while wailing loudly;
others rolled their eyes or twisted their knees about as they wailed loudly.
Some pressed their thighs with their hands as if their feet were being scorched, wailing and weeping loudly;
others cried out: "Alas, Buddha!"
"Alas, Buddha! they cried out, wailing loudly;
some wiped their eyes with their hands, while others rubbed their faces with their hands, wailing loudly.
The arrow of suffering pierced their hearts; they wailed with choked sobs, and overcome by pain, grief, and distress, they could not compose themselves and wept aloud.
Thus, tears fell like rain from immeasurable thousands of billions of sentient beings as they sighed deeply and repeatedly fainted before regaining consciousness.
Some pressed their palms together, their tears flowing freely as they wailed;
some propped their heads with their right hands, weeping as they sank down and collapsed to the ground, crying out loudly;
others struck their heads with their left hands, consumed by the fire of despondency and grief, crying out loudly.
Some, their bodies withered and emaciated, writhed in distress and wailed aloud;
others threw up both hands, their faces losing their natural color, and, fainting and choked with sobs, wailed aloud.
At that time, those devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, each with their retinues, rushed toward the place where the Buddha was.

Having reached the Buddha’s presence, they all prostrated themselves on the ground before him like felled trees; some bowed at the Buddha’s feet, some cried out loudly, some wailed and rolled about on the ground, and some, standing before the Buddha with both arms raised, clasped one another’s hands, wailing and weeping while crying out these words: “Alas, O Buddha!”
Alas, Great Honored One!
Alas, Dharma! Alas, Great Compassion!
Alas, Great Abode! Alas, Great Refuge! Have pity on us and protect us!

The Eye of the Three Realms has lost its way and shown us the path; now the entire world shall become desolate, and all sentient beings shall be blind and sightless. The bright torch of Great Wisdom is extinguished forever this day.

They grasped and pulled at one another like those who have lost their parents, relatives, brothers, sisters, sons, or daughters; thus they wailed and choked with grief, crying out with loud lamentations.
Or they may speak thus:
"Alas, our Honored One! Alas, our great spiritual friend!"
Alas, how skillful his eloquence and subtle, beautiful speech!
Alas, how his gait is like that of the lion king!
Alas, how his gait is like that of the great bull king!
"Alas! Your gait was like that of the Great Elephant King!
Alas! You are the Dharma King who eloquently expounds the nectar of immortality!

With such various and immeasurable words of lamentation, they wailed and wept with piercing grief; some threw themselves from the sky to the ground, fainting and writhing, sobbing and crying out in sorrow.

At that time, Ānanda fainted and fell prostrate to the ground like a tree cut down. After a long while, he regained consciousness; standing before the Buddha with both hands pressed to the earth, he gazed up at the World-Honored One without averting his eyes for a moment and spoke these verses:
“My affliction and distress redouble, Seeing all these sentient beings Pierced by the arrows of suffering, Wailing piteously and weeping aloud.”
For example, like merchants on a path shrouded in darkness who are plundered by bandits,
suddenly seeing the brilliance of a great fire illuminating those before them,
their great terror increases further; they have no means to flee.
In this place of contact, there is no refuge, for one beholds a mass of fire.
Since the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, the great multitude is filled with sorrow and suffering;
thus, these unprotected ones are further pierced by the arrows of pain.
The World-Honored One does not remain in the world, and others have likewise entered parinirvāṇa.
Now that the Most Excellent Person has passed away, how can I bear to behold this?
He emitted a great, blazing radiance, like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted.
Having fallen to the state of a Malla, how could I bear to see it?
Now I shall never again see him as he was when he preached the Dharma as usual beneath the Bamboo Grove and in the Jeta Grove.
How did he enter Vaiśālī, the preeminent city of the Licchavis, and speak to the Licchavis: "The Supreme Person has passed into parinirvāṇa"?
How did he enter Kapilavastu, the preeminent city of the Śākyas?
Why do you address him with such unpleasant words, saying that the Supreme Person has entered parinirvāṇa?
Why have you gone to Ajātaśatru, the eminent king of Magadha,
and why do you speak these words, saying that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa?
Thousands upon thousands of beings weep again and again;
how can they be consoled when the Lion of the Śākyas has passed into parinirvāṇa?
So too the bhikṣus, the bhikṣuṇīs, and all those of the lay community.
How did you speak these words, "The King of the Śākyas has passed into parinirvāṇa"?
Whether while walking in meditation, or when entering great meditative absorption,
or when questioned by devas and nāgas— how could you, who are fearless, have said this?
"Ānanda! Where is the Buddha, the most supreme field of merit?
After the elders had thus questioned him, what did I, the World-Honored One, reply?
For whom have I prepared this great lion throne?
And for whom have I prepared this great lion couch?
Among the assembly, I am without fear, like the roar of a great lion.
Furthermore, from whom did you hear the most profound and peerless Dharma?
For whom did you wash your feet?
And for whom did you hold the *kāṣāya* robe?
After the Supreme Person has passed away, for whom will [the Dharma] be upheld?
And who, before the great assembly, will praise my diligent efforts?
And who will further praise me as a great ocean of vast learning and wisdom?
"O you of great wisdom and eloquence!
You bring joy to boundless multitudes; to whom else shall I now turn to hear such subtle, gentle, and beautiful words?
Having thus lamented, that son of the Buddha who hears and upholds [the Dharma]—
"Standing at the side of the Buddha's feet, he fell to the ground in a swoon.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Son of Gautamī!"
There is no sorrow more grievous and no delusion more profound than this. I have already told you this truth in the past:

"All those one loves must eventually be parted from; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, like a dream, like an illusion, like a mirage, like a bubble, like foam, like dew—false and unsubstantial. Conditioned phenomena are likewise so."
"You already know this, son of Gotamī! You should rise now;
you must go at once and prepare a couch for the Tathāgata between the twin trees, with the head toward the east, the head raised like a cow's head;
facing directly north, with his right hand supporting his cheek."

Beneath the twin trees, specifically toward the southern side, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, shall enter parinirvāṇa during the latter part of this night, extinguishing all conditioned constituents without remainder; this is his parinirvāṇa.

At that time, Ānanda wept, wailed, lamented, and was overcome with grief and distress; his face was covered in tears as he followed the World-Honored One’s command and prepared a lion throne at the site of the twin śāla trees.
Having finished spreading it out, he spoke these verses:
"I have now prepared this final Great Seer’s lion-throne;
henceforth, no more shall be spread for the Most Excellent One to lie upon."
How can I bear to see that, within the twin trees of the empty forest,
after the Most Victorious One has passed away, the World-Honored One is silent and no longer seen?
May the various forest-dwelling deities who protect this grove not have to guard it in vain through the long night.
No longer seeing the Tathāgata, how could one find joy in dwelling here?
Alas for the nature of impermanence! Like an illusion, a dream, or a bubble, the Great Man, the Teacher of Men, shall today enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha spoke these verses to Ānanda:
“The Tathāgata has already declared: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent;
Dependent on causes and conditions, they lack autonomy. You must strengthen your resolve and do not grieve.”
"How can it be that because of your grief and sorrow, and your weeping, the fact of impermanence has already occurred? Let the wise not be deluded or distressed.
Having spoken these words, Ānanda then replied to the Great Venerable Nīloda with a verse:
“Fearless Aniruddha! Do not speak such words.
Beholding the passing away of the Supreme Person, how could the Venerable One be without sorrow?
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha again replied to Ānanda in verse:
"Do my eyes have no tears?
I restrain them out of deliberate forbearance.
Seeing the myriad classes of sentient beings, most of whom are oppressed by craving,"
Furthermore, with my divine eye I see sentient beings afflicted by various sufferings;
out of great compassion for them, I should weep.
It is for the benefit of the world, not out of personal anguish.
"Therefore, I say to you, noble one: do not grieve; you should keep the Dharma in mind.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, and a multitude of hundreds of thousands of billions—including devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, asuras, and garuḍas—surrounded the World-Honored One as he proceeded to the Śāla grove.
Having arrived, he lay on his right side upon the lion-couch.

Once the World-Honored One had lain upon that lion-couch, celestial flowers and celestial powdered incense immediately rained down from the void, and hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music were played. Furthermore, they brought various human flowers, various powdered incenses, various ointments, and various sounds to make offerings to the World-Honored One, planting roots of wholesome merit, each proclaiming aloud:
"This is the final reclining of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is also our final opportunity to behold the World-Honored One during this kṣaṇa, lava, and muhūrta."
At that time, in the eastern direction, there was a world named Ratnanirghoṣeśvara, ten thousand koṭis of buddha-fields away from this buddha-field.
In that land, there was a Buddha named Siṃhanādanirghoṣa, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

In that world there was a bodhisattva named Śubhārthacintin, who, having descended from that realm, came to this land to be born by transformation within the palace of King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, in Rājagṛha, the city of the kingdom of Magadha, where he sat cross-legged.
Once he was born, he spoke this verse:
"I have come from the Tathāgata’s buddha-field, The Lion’s Roar;
hearing that there is a World-Honored One here, The Lion of the Śākyas, dwelling in this world."
At that time, a devaputra in the air replied to the Bodhisattva Kalyāṇārthacintin with a verse:
"Now that King of Men, the World-Honored One, the Lion of the Śākyas,
desires to enter nirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees."
When these words had been spoken, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kalyāṇārthacintin immediately replied to that deva in verse:
“From incalculable Buddha-fields, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis,
I have come from those lands to hear the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas.”
Encountering his desire to pass into parinirvāṇa, he was about to proceed between the twin trees.
My coming here to this buddha-field was not in vain;
I have now arrived at this place just as that Honored One is about to enter nirvāṇa.
All the worlds, including the devas, are filled with sorrow, how much more so for me?
This single thought-moment does not endure; I should quickly see the World-Honored One, lest my journey here be in vain and I fail to behold the Buddha.
Sudassana, having exhorted the King of Magadha with words of righteous counsel, spoke these compassionate, beautiful, and virtuous words to make his heart rejoice:
"Great King, listen to my words: A Great Being has appeared in the world."
O King, do not let your mind run wild; go quickly to where the Buddha dwells.
In many thousands of billions of eons, one might encounter him but once;
now that you have met this Teacher, O wise one, do not let this moment pass in vain.
I pray that Your Majesty do not harbor doubts, thinking me a foolish child;
I am no foolish child, but it is Your Majesty who is but a child,
for you were greedy for worldly pleasures and committed the calamity of parricide.
This is the folly of a child; he shall surely fall into the evil realms.
The King has drawn near to evil associates, such as Devadatta, who incites strife and discord.
Following that rebellious mind, he has killed his faultless father.
The King was peerless in accordance with the Dharma and was truly a compeer among the sons of the Buddha;
yet, because he harbored a self-centered mind and lacked wisdom, he gave rise to rebellion.
Such a great and heinous act of parricide is a matter of no small terror.
Because of this, the king will surely fall into the great Avīci Hell.
While the Buddha is still present in the world and has not yet entered parinirvāṇa,
you should give rise to a mind of offering toward the Buddha’s various relic bones.
I pray that the King grant me his joyful permission; I wish to go to the presence of the Buddha.
Having been born in this land, I do not seek to enjoy various sensual desires.
Because I have heard of my native land and of the Tathāgata Siṃhanāda, I have come here.
Praising this Great Seer, who has entered parinirvāṇa like a lion,
they have come to be born in this land in order to pay him homage;
all the kṣatriya kinsmen have simultaneously approached the Buddha.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru addressed the youth with these verses:
"The site where the Malla was born is far from here; One must not go lightly, for it requires a grand carriage.
Youth, you need only wait tonight; Tomorrow, having arrayed the troops, you may proceed in peace."
At that time, the youth Kalyāṇamati replied to King Ajātaśatru with these verses:
"Great King, do not give way to indolence; My supernormal powers are inconceivable.
If I now wish to travel toward the east, There are immeasurable Buddha-fields, yet none are obstructed."
From the buddha-fields where you originally came, You have traversed immeasurable and boundless realms;
The buddha-lands therein are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges— How could the birthplace of the Malla hero be far?
At that time, the youth rose from King Ajātaśatru’s lap and proceeded on foot; he departed calmly from the city of Rājagṛha and spoke these verses:

“If you wish to behold the Buddha, who is pure and beyond reproach, The one of great power, the most excellent person capable of subduing all, Follow me quickly to see him, Before that Śākya Sage enters into parinirvāṇa.”

At that time, having departed from Rājagṛha on foot, within the brief span of a kṣaṇa or a lava, he was surrounded by an assembly of seventy-two thousand people; furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless hundreds of billions of nayutas of devas who followed the youth to the place where the Buddha was, desiring to prostrate at the Tathāgata’s feet.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had lain on his right side like a lion among men, in an interval of a kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, there was a buddha-field five hundred thousand koṭis of buddha-worlds away from this buddha-field in the southern direction. In that buddha-field dwelt a Tathāgata named Ratnākara-suvyūha, endowed with the ten titles.

There was a bodhisattva named Śāntivikrama who, passing away from that land, was reborn in this world, within the city of Śrāvastī on the Jambudvīpa continent, into the family of the great householder Siṃha.
Immediately upon his birth, he spoke these verses:
"Throughout how many billions of kalpas, I have severed my hands and feet, plucked out my eyes, and split open my body; I have cut off immeasurable heads."
Wives, concubines, sons, and daughters, as well as all manner of wealth and treasures—
for ten billion kalpas, they sought unsurpassed bodhi.
To deliver all living beings, they practiced extensive giving and cultivated merit.
"Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, such an eye as yours is rare.
Then, the householder Siṃhaka replied to the youth in verse:
"Are you a deva or a nāga? Are you a yakṣa or a rākṣasa?"
At the very moment of your birth, you spoke words with perfect clarity.
My entire retinue was struck with terror and fled in all directions;
yet, upon hearing the Buddha’s name, I did not run away.
At that time, the youth replied to the householder in verse:
"I am neither a deva nor a nāga, nor a yakṣa or a rākṣasa.
You, O householder, do not know; you think I am a man of the world."
I speak of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
I am the God among Gods; O householder, you should know this.
At that time, Siṃhaka replied to the youth in verse:
"My mind is filled with further doubt, and I am struck with wonder, O youth,
having heard such words from you, which are like the speech of the wise."
What are the devas and nāgas, the yakṣas and kiṃnaras?
What is the God among Gods?
O Youth, explain this once more.
At that time, the youth replied to the householder in verse:
"To the south of this realm, there is a Buddha named Ratnākara;
currently dwelling there like a lion, it is from that place that I have come."
A hundred times I have been Śakra, and I have also come as a sovereign lord;
a hundred times I have been Brahmā, and I have also been a wheel-turning monarch.
I could speak of this for a long time—for an eon or even a hundred million eons.
"It cannot be fully described; let the wise quickly approach the Buddha.
"So be it, Great Householder!
You should constantly cultivate such practice of the Dharma, drawing near to it, keeping it in mind, and extensively revealing it to others."
"Great Householder!
What is the practice of the Dharma?

The Tathāgata shall now explain it. Those Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Ratnakūṭa and Subhūti, who are fully endowed with the ten titles of a Tathāgata, have accomplished three dharmas; they have attained non-retrogression regarding the mind of awakening and shall swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi."
"What are these three?
First, entering the boundless mind; second, entering profound wisdom; and third, entering the samādhi of firm practice.
At that time, the youth, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one wishes to enter into profound wisdom, which is cherished and revered by gods and worldlings alike,
there is only the Great Renown of the Buddhas, who are well able to know causes and non-causes."
In those words, there is nothing that is not awakening; this wisdom has no place for attachment.
Having abandoned all attachments and removed the poisoned arrow, one realizes the Dharma-wisdom and attains Buddhahood.
Mindfulness of the mind is boundless and yet has no mind; entering such a mind, one attains tranquility.
To accord with this mind is called "entering," and this mind is said to pervade all things.
If it were broken or cut, it would not be solid; the Tathāgata has taught that all phenomena are without breaking.
All existents have a nature like space; such is true thusness, like a diamond.

One should know that such intrinsic nature is empty; if one can practice this without attachment, one will then escape the net of afflictions and attain perfect enlightenment, free from all states of existence.
One should know that there is no knowing of anything; one should realize that there is nothing to be realized;
one should awaken to the fact that there is nothing to be awakened to; and regarding all sounds heard, one should have no grasping or attachment.
Entering the profound Dharma, they have no notion of dharmas; Liberating sentient beings, they have no notion of liberation;
In vast quiescence, there is no notion of vast quiescence; Attaining the realization of Bodhi, they have no notion of a path.
Those truly heroic ones have removed the poisoned arrow; They fully comprehend all the destinies of sentient beings.
"Because he knows all things, he is called a Buddha; he is difficult to approach lightly and remains unattached.

At that time, having spoken this verse, in the space of a kṣaṇa, lava, and muhūrta, the householder Siṃha, together with his retinue of two hundred people surrounding him on all sides, immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, dedicated it toward enlightenment, and attained the patience of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, eighteen billion devaputras also gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, reaching ultimate enlightenment without ever regressing.
Furthermore, four *nayuta* of sentient beings, having become free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the youth spoke again in verse:
"I have not come here in vain; I have gone to the presence of the Lion of the Śākyas."
Within the terrors of birth and death, he delivers tens of millions of beings.
There are many such sentient beings who have already resolved for Bodhi,
abiding in supreme equanimity and attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
My father abides in the patience of the Dharma; my mother, my elder brother, my kinsmen, and eighteen billion devas all abide on the path to Bodhi.
"I have obtained great wealth and treasures, immeasurable and inconceivable;
I am drawing closer to the Buddha-Dharma and am gradually moving far away from poverty.

At that time, after the youth Śāntivardhana had converted his parents and their retinue, he departed from the great city of Śrāvastī. Surrounded on all sides by his parents, his various kinsmen, and hundreds of thousands of countless sentient beings, he proceeded before the multitude toward the Śāla Grove, the birthplace of the Malla clan, desiring to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and behold the World-Honored One.

At that time, while the Tathāgata was lying on his right side upon the lion throne, during that very kṣaṇa, lava, and muhūrta, there was a Buddha named Ruciraghoṣa, endowed with the ten titles, residing in a buddha-field eight hundred million times ten thousand buddha-fields to the west of this world.

In that buddha-field there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Apratiṣṭhita (No-Object-of-Attachment). Having vanished from his body in that buddha-field, he was suddenly born by transformation within the home of a great householder named Śubhagupta, in the great city of Vārāṇasī on the land of Jambudvīpa in this buddha-field.
At the very moment of his birth, the youth Apratiṣṭhita spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are without a point of reference; The deluded are driven by their perceptions.
They do not escape manifold sufferings, But cause all their anxieties and afflictions to increase."
All phenomena have no location; though one seeks them, they cannot be found.
Whether exhausted or not exhausted, all things are non-existent.
Space has nothing upon which it relies; even that which is not space has no reliance.
The dharmas of emptiness have no causes and conditions, yet causes and conditions are not non-existent either.
Those various teachings he has proclaimed are profound, hidden, and difficult to perceive;
there is indeed one who can explain them: the Honored among Men, the Lion of the Śākyas.
Like a great elephant or a great lion, like Brahmā free from all desires,
today at the twin śāla trees, he shall extinguish the Eye of the World.
Standing amidst the great assembly, he is like the moon on the fifteenth day.
He preached the sublime Dharma for the multitude, yet he can no longer be seen.
Surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus, like Śakra atop the mountain peak,
from this day forth he shall not enter again any of the wondrous cities.
The most honored among gods and humans, the supreme one who beats the Dharma drum, has uttered sounds that gladden the multitude; we shall never hear them again.
"There is no self, there is no agent"—thus did the Tathāgata teach this Dharma.
"Now I wish to enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Aśrayaparāvṛtti (No-Grasping) had spoken this verse, a thousand followers in the city of Vārāṇasī said:

"This youth is most marvelous and rare; his wisdom, eloquence, and fearlessness are profound. Having been born, he was able to remember the events of his past lives, and he could skillfully speak various sublime verses. He possesses such great power and wisdom, fearless and invincible, with pure and wondrous eloquence. We pray that we may attain such wisdom as this youth."

At that time, the youth Anālamba, wishing to lead the great assembly into the stage of non-retrogression—a unique dharma not found in the world, rare and difficult to encounter, immeasurable and boundless—caused them to enter it, and likewise caused them to attain the dharma of the endurance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the great assembly addressed the youth, saying: "Excellent, O youth!"
"We shall now follow this youth to that place to behold the World-Honored One and also to make offerings.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Aśrayaṇika, together with his retinue and assembly of hundreds of thousands, surrounded him with reverence as they stood before him; they departed from the great city of Vārāṇasī and proceeded directly to the Buddha’s dwelling, desiring to behold and make offerings to him.

At that time, during that very kṣaṇa, lava, and muhūrta, to the north of this buddha-field, beyond sixty-four thousand koṭis of buddha-fields, there was a Buddha named Vihārabodhipakṣaparivartana Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles.

In that buddha-field there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Vikāśita-ṛddhiguṇa; passing away from that realm, he was reborn in this land of Jambudvīpa, within the great city of Vaiśālī, spontaneously appearing by transformation in the household of the general Siṃha.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vikasita-ṛddhiguṇa had been born into that family, he immediately spoke these verses:
"Have you heard of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Who increases the clan of the Śākyas,
And delivers from all calamities and hardships Countless hundreds of thousands of billions?"
I have heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is an ocean of boundless wisdom;
through diligence and meditative concentration, he has profoundly reached the further shore.
The Tathāgata has extracted the poisoned arrow and attained a mind of patience, gentle and well-tamed.
He constantly preaches the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, yet he does not cling to the marks of phenomena.
Have you heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not cling to the three realms?
Whether worldly actions are performed or not, his wisdom pervades all things.
"The desire realm and the form realm, even unto the formless realm—
if one can weigh and measure these with wisdom, does that eye exist? At that time,
a celestial maiden named Bodhipakṣaparivartinī from the household of the Great General transformed herself into human form, appeared before the youth, and replied to him in verse:
“The World-Honored One shall remain for an eon, or perhaps even longer than an eon;
you shall see the Buddha later, but for now, enjoy the five desires.
Partake of excellent and sublime fortune and rank, just like those of a great royal house.”
"Various kinds of wondrous sounds, songs, dances, and performances.
At that time, the youth, fully knowing that the Tathāgata had already benefited sentient beings and that the roots of goodness of all devas and humans were perfected, replied to the goddess in verse:
"Those foolish sentient beings take pleasure in the delights of the five desires."
I have not heard of the Perfectly Enlightened One, nor of the Buddha’s teachings.
I do not accept the five desires; the five desires lack solidity.
The five desires are like swords and blades—who could truly believe in them?
Pigs, dogs, and jackals, mules, horses, oxen, and donkeys—
these kinds of beings crave the five desires and are censured by the Buddhas and their śrāvakas;
they are blind, sightless, with impaired faculties, deformed, ugly, and crippled.
Such forms of sensual desire as these are censured by all Buddhas and Śrāvakas.
Whether it be ants, butterflies, flies, *kṛmi* insects, or peacocks—
those who engage in such lustful conduct— I censure them because I am superior to them.
Just as a great pit of fire, blazing and filling Jambudvīpa, into which a blind man might fall—so too is sensual desire.
All desires are impermanent and suffering; they are censured by the wise.
If a person does not recognize their own faults, such as these are driven by desire.
I do not accept the five sensual pleasures; this the World-Honored One has already realized.
Those who are able to hear this meaning should know them to be like the Buddha.
I have heard from the Buddha that, during the final watch of the night, that Buddha, the King of Mountains Sumeru, shall pass into parinirvāṇa.
Let us go quickly to him who has exhausted all fetters.
Those who wish to see him may go, for I fear that the World-Honored One will pass into extinction.
The Supreme Person has taught these most excellent factors of enlightenment;
even in hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, it is difficult to encounter them and plant roots of goodness.
If one visits the abode of Nirvāṇa, beholds the Honored One of the Śākya clan,
and hears the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas, one shall plant the seeds of goodness.
Whether they be devas, humans, or yakṣas, if they go to the presence of the Tathāgata, [they shall likewise do so].
"If you love the banner of the Śākya clan, quickly behold the one of great renown.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kumārabhūta Vikrīḍitābhijñaguṇa had spoken this verse, surrounded on all sides by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings and standing at the head of the assembly, he departed from Vaiśālī and went directly to where the Buddha was, desiring to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and to pay homage and make offerings to him in person.
The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Four Youthful Boys, Volume One;
The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Four Youthful Boys, Volume Two.
Translated during the Sui Dynasty by [the monk from] Gandhāra in North India.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta.
At that time, the World-Honored One was reclining on his right side upon a lion bed.

Then, four youths came from the four directions, each surrounded before and behind by a great multitude; leading the assembly, they were all equal in wisdom, supernatural powers, majestic virtue, and religious practice, with no difference between them even as small as a hair’s breadth. Together they proceeded to where the Buddha was, and having arrived before the Buddha, they joined their palms in reverent salutation.

When those four youths arrived before the Buddha, each was accompanied by the retinues from their respective cities and towns, as well as all devas and humans and hundreds of thousands of beings of various kinds; they all joined their palms, composed their minds, and with joyful exultation, bowed their bodies in reverence toward the four youths.

When those four youths arrive, for a distance of one yojana in length and breadth across the four directions, the devas will rain down flowers until they completely cover the ground; celestial music of hundreds of thousands of varieties will resound, and the devas will sing songs of praise in immeasurable numbers.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha spontaneously manifested four lion thrones, clearly appearing in the four directions.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions do four couches appear on the right side of the All-Knowing One’s four quarters, with a vast lion seat spread upon them?”
Having spoken these words, the Buddha said to Ānanda: “Ānanda,
have you seen these four youths?”

Coming from the four directions, his face was like the full moon; surpassing the radiance of the sun, he eclipsed the four continents. His majestic virtue was exceptionally sublime, his teeth were white and brilliantly radiant. He emitted the light of wisdom and attained great diligence; entering into profound knowledge, he accomplished meritorious virtues. With consciousness and wisdom thoroughly penetrating, he possessed deep faith and practice; humble and modest, his conduct and deeds were perfected. His insight was far-reaching as he attained right mindfulness and concentration. Possessing skillful wisdom and great expedient means, he held the foremost dhāraṇī. For the sake of all sentient beings, he preached the Dharma in accordance with their needs, increasing their roots of goodness, having planted various roots of merit under immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.

Each dwelling in one of the four directions, they have each heard of my parinirvāṇa within their own buddha-fields; having each sought instruction and made requests before the Tathāgatas of those fields, they have been born in this land desiring to hear and see me, and to learn of the matters concerning the merit of my teaching the Dharma and its benefits. Behold today, during the final watch of the night, how the Tathāgata—among the twin śāla trees at the birthplace of the Mallas—is about to enter the remainderless nirvāṇa, the inconceivable nirvāṇa, the peerless nirvāṇa of all worlds, the rare nirvāṇa of all worlds, the nirvāṇa of peace and happiness for all worlds, the invincible nirvāṇa of all worlds, and the pure nirvāṇa that severs and leaves behind all realms of existence; it is thus that the Tathāgata shall attain this subtle, wondrous, and supreme nirvāṇa.

“Ānanda! This youth coming from the eastern direction has a subtle and exquisite complexion, is endowed with great merit, is upright and pleasing to behold, and his radiance shines everywhere. His majestic power is blazing like a great fire emitting vast light; surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of followers and a multitude of billions of devas who all offer him worship, he receives flowers raining down from heaven as he approaches the Buddha’s dwelling, desiring to make offerings to the Buddha.”

“Ānanda! This youth was once a wheel-turning sage king in the land of that Tathāgata Siṃhaghoṣasvara; he ruled over a thousand worlds with sovereign mastery and was venerated by all devas and humans.”

During his time of governing and transforming [the world], he constantly preached the Dharma extensively among the heavens of the desire realm and among human beings. He upheld the words and meanings of the teachings and expounded their subtle principles for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings. He enabled them to plant various roots of goodness, attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and master the practice of the Dharma. He was praised by the multitude of sages as boundless and uninterrupted; having attained the most supreme and subtle power of fearlessness, he entered deeply into the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and achieved eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Through skillful wisdom, he reached the further shore of boundless wisdom.

Having fulfilled such practices of these dharmas, he ruled according to the Dharma for eighteen *koṭis* of years, without using weapons or staffs to afflict sentient beings, and without craving the royal throne out of desire for sensual pleasures. During those eighteen *koṭis* of years, he brought eighteen *nayutas* of sentient beings to maturity, establishing them in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and causing them to attain the stage of non-retrogression in the bodhisattva-dharmas.

Once that son of good family has attained the stage of non-retrogression from his initial resolve, until he finally achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that king likewise, at a later time, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and leaves the home life for homelessness.
"Immediately after going forth, he practiced the holy life for eighty-one billion years.
From the time he went forth, he never sat or lay down, much less slept."

For eighty-one billion years, he did not give rise to even a single thought of desire or a mind of anger; how much less could there be thoughts of killing or causing affliction? He was free from unwholesome deeds as well as notions of hatred or affection.
Furthermore, they do not conceive thoughts of practicing or not practicing.
They constantly abide in two dharmas; what are these two?
First, although they have attained the fleshly eye, they have no conception of a "fleshly eye."
Although he was able to discern and know the various aggregates of phenomena, he did not grasp at or cling to the conceptualization of those aggregates.
During those eighty-one billion years, he spoke no further of anything that was unbeneficial or any other extraneous matters.

Whether it be the perception of earth, water, fire, or wind; the perception of space or consciousness; the perception of woman or man; the perception of hunger and thirst; the perception of a village, a secluded place, or a city and its environs; perceptions of opposition or non-opposition; perceptions of seclusion or meditative concentration; the perception of self or other; the perception of form or formlessness; the perception of extremes or the middle; the perception of arising or ceasing; the perception of the small or the great—may all such various other distracted perceptions be entirely stilled and extinguished, so that no further discrimination arises;
except for the twenty treasuries of the Dharma-fund, which one should contemplate and cultivate.

“In that interval, they brought eighty thousand *nayutas* of sentient beings to maturity, establishing them definitively in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; all those beings had first resolved their minds toward enlightenment in this very realm.

In a single *kṣaṇa-lava*, they traveled with sovereign ease from that buddha-field to various other buddha-fields, arriving at the abodes of the World-Honored Ones in those realms to pay homage and serve them.

In each of those worlds and each of those buddha-fields, they arrived with a single body; there was no duality or simultaneity in their singular person or singular activity, for in each of those lands, the Buddhas were all identical.”

In this very instant, at this very *lava*, he lies upon his right side; on this same day, during the final watch of the night, he shall enter *nirvāṇa* between a pair of *śāla* trees in the birthplace of the Mallas. All these Tathāgatas, like that Tathāgata, are named Śākyamuni, fully endowed with the ten titles; those Buddhas likewise appear in an age of five corruptions.

“Ānanda! By means of such an immeasurable, boundless, and unobstructed physical eye of right knowledge and right vision, I perceive that which is not accessible to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others, for it is not within their sphere.”

Ānanda! If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who hear this Dharma-gate, and having heard it, give rise to faith, admiring my wisdom of right knowledge and vision with my physical eyes and desiring to attain this wisdom—even unto the fulfillment of all-knowledge—and if they give rise to a single thought of right faith, maintaining it in succession without abandoning it, then as soon as they have given rise to that thought, they shall produce an immeasurable accumulation of merit; how much more so if they attain an immeasurable and boundless mass of great virtue?

“Ānanda! If there were good sons or good daughters who, for eighteen nayutas of Tathāgatas and for eighteen nayuta-billions of years, were to provide offerings, show respect, honor, and praise with all manner of pleasant requisites, and personally serve those Tathāgatas—though the merit they obtain during those eighteen nayutas of years is immeasurable, it still cannot compare to the merit produced by the mind of aspiration upon hearing this Dharma-gate; it is beyond all analogy.”
“Ānanda! This youth, within a single day and night in my Dharma, has taught and benefited immeasurable sentient beings; how much more so the benefit he will accomplish over a long period of time?”
If Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the other śrāvakas were unable to bring about such great benefit and deliver such immeasurable sentient beings as this, [it would not be so].

“Ānanda! Suppose you and all others were to spend your entire lifespans teaching and transforming sentient beings with many discourses, never thinking of anything else and resting neither by day nor by night; even though you were to provide such benefit through teaching, you yourselves would still be unable to shoulder the heavy burden of the Buddha-dharma within my teaching.”
"What you see now is what this youth who has come here is carrying.
He spoke again, saying: "It is so, Ānanda!"
In this way, the youth brings great benefit to all sentient beings; endowed with compassion, he keeps sentient beings in mind and seeks their welfare, for this youth possesses immeasurable merit.
“Ānanda! Have you seen the youth coming from the south?

Like the full moon on the fifteenth night of autumn, his radiance is blazing and intense; holding a staff adorned with various jewels in his right hand, he strikes this great earth. Having struck the great earth, he utters these words:”
For example, suppose there were a precious vessel in the kingdom of Magadha— made either of gold or silver— which, having been completed,
was well-polished and refined, free from dust and grime, free from flaws or cracks,
free from leaks, excellent, bright and pure, and devoid of dirt or grease.
Accomplished through various causes, conditions, and manifold matters; refined by various functional powers; clear and pure in five locations, fully endowed with ten locations;
far removed from the thousandfold scrutiny of observation, and far removed from the dross of gold and silver in the twelve locations;
its lineage is authentic, its golden nature most excellent, perfected through a hundred refinements, and newly forged.
Once completed, it was fully equipped with eight hundred thousand skilled artisans who gazed upon it with single-minded attention;
it was entirely free from dust, grease, filth, or any obscuration. When struck, this wondrous vessel produced a sound such that anyone who heard it could extinguish all suffering.
“Ānanda! Such is the analogy, such is the sound of the vessel; I have merely spoken of it briefly.
Yet the sound produced when this youth strikes the great earth with his staff, which is adorned and purified by the interlacing of various jewels, is likewise so.”

“Ānanda! This youth is named Śāntamati; he is a great bodhisattva mahāsattva who has come from the buddha-field of Ratnakūṭa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, located in the southern direction.”
That Buddha-world is named Ratnavyūha. "Ānanda, what do you think?"
For what reason is that world named Ratnavyūha?
Ānanda! In that Buddha-world, there is not a single sentient being who dwells in the state of non-determination, nor is there anyone of wrong determination.
Ānanda! All those sentient beings are firmly established in the certainty of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Ānanda! That land is a bodhisattva-land; the sentient beings in that land have no conception of male or female. Ānanda!

All those sentient beings practice the holy life (brahmacarya); they are free from all defiled desires, their wisdom and conduct are pure, and even the name of "defiled desire" does not exist among them. Ānanda!

Among all those sentient beings who adorn that Buddha-field, there are none with unwholesome thoughts, nor do they have any thought of food; they have only two kinds of sustenance. What are these two?
First, they take meditative concentration and wisdom as their food; second, they take the joy of the Dharma as their food. Ānanda!
In that buddha-field, the five aggregates are not taught, nor are the three vehicles; there, only the aggregate of omniscience and the bodhisattva treasury are extensively expounded.
Ānanda! For this reason, that buddha-world is named Ratnavyūha. Ānanda!

Regarding all those beings from other Buddha-fields who are born in this land, as well as those who aspire to be born in that Buddha-field—may all such beings who so aspire never regress from their progress toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Ānanda! There may be bodhisattvas who come from other buddha-fields to be born there; once born, they are able to know for themselves all matters within that buddha-field. Those bodhisattvas, having also been born there, immediately—in a single kṣaṇa, lava, or muhūrta—each conceive the thought that their own bodies are the Buddha.

“Ānanda! That Tathāgata Ratnākara extensively expounded for those immeasurable and boundless nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others the Dharma-gate of all-knowledge and the Bodhisattva-treasury; he did so without interruption and spoke nothing else.”

Ānanda! Even if I were to spend immeasurable thousands of kalpas describing the merits of that buddha-field, as well as detailing each of the supreme dharmas attained by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—namely, their vows to adorn the buddha-field—I could not reach the end of them.
Ānanda, I have merely briefly described the names of the merits of that Buddha-world.

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntivikrama has come from that direction because he wishes to behold my entry into parinirvāṇa, and furthermore, out of compassion for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, so that they may resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Furthermore, it is to manifest the matters of the meritorious adornments of that buddha-field;
and furthermore, it is to manifest the fame of the benefits brought about by the appearance of that Buddha Ratnakūṭa.

That is to say, it is to manifest the great deeds of the Dharma-practice of all bodhisattvas and to proclaim the matter of his true renown, desiring that the immeasurable and boundless sentient beings of this world-system may embrace the True Dharma. Thus, he has come to this buddha-field of Śākyamuni in order to inspire a heart of joy in all bodhisattvas of the future.

“Ānanda! In the past, when this youth was practicing the bodhisattva path, he encountered the appearance of Dīpaṃkara Buddha in the world; at that time, he had been a universal monarch named Duryodhana.”
“Ānanda! At that time, the noble King Arjuna preached the True Dharma for immeasurable billions of boundless sentient beings, bringing their roots of goodness to maturity.

From the first light of dawn until the mealtime, that noble king transformed and delivered thirty-six billion sentient beings, establishing them in the stage of non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, causing them to enter the assembly of those fixed in rightness and realize the dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).”
After that Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara had entered parinirvāṇa, this holy king exerted great diligence, shaved off his hair and beard, and left the household life for homelessness.
After he had gone forth into homelessness, for a full thousand years, he continued the turning of the True Dharma Wheel of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.

That Holy King benefited immeasurable and boundless sentient beings; having performed these benefits, at a later time, during the hour when the sun was setting, he further transformed thirty-six billion sentient beings, causing them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, at that same time when the sun set, he caused seventy thousand *nayutas* of sentient beings to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) and become *arhats*, let alone the incalculable number of those on the path of realization who had seen the Truth and were still in training (*śaikṣa*).

“Ānanda! Even if I were to use the wisdom of a Buddha to describe the deeds this youth, the Bodhisattva Śāntivarta, performed for the benefit of sentient beings in the past, I could not reach their end.”
Ānanda! For the sake of this youth Citta-viśuddha, you should prepare and arrange a seat before me; by doing so, you shall obtain immeasurable, boundless, and most excellent merit.
“If there are sentient beings who hear the name of this Bodhisattva Śāntavikrāmin, those sentient beings will be no different from seeing the Buddha in person right now. Ānanda!

Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the names of this Dharma-fundamental of the Adorned Prophecy, should give rise to even a single thought of pure faith—whether out of a desire to see that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnakūṭa appearing before them, or out of a desire to welcome him, prostrate to him, attend upon him, and make offerings to him—anyone who thus resolves their mind or desires to hear the Dharma: Ānanda!
I now bestow upon them all the prediction of enlightenment, that they shall be reborn in that land, where they may behold the Tathāgata and hear the True Dharma.
The bodhisattvas born within that buddha-field also desire to practice those same dharmic deeds, with the sole exception of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess the power of vows.

Ānanda! Those sentient beings have well attained a great benefit if they can even hear the names of this Dharma-source of the adornment of merit as it is being spoken, reaching their ears; how much more so if, having heard them, they attain pure faith?
“Ānanda! These Dharma phrases are such as they truly are, not false; you should well protect, well attend to, and remember them. Why is this so, Ānanda?”
Have the people of Jambudvīpa never before heard such sūtra passages and names? Ānanda!
As for those who are nominal bodhisattvas and those who slander the Dharma—do not let such people as these hear them.
Why is this? It is because the offense of slandering the Dharma is vast and profoundly grave. "Ānanda!
"Do you see this palanquin, adorned with various jewels, coming through the air from the western direction?
Have you seen it? Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "I have indeed seen it."
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"Do you see that young boy among them?

Through the miraculous transformations of his two feet, he has leaped into the air and come flying here, shaking this great earth—shaking it greatly, trembling it greatly. When the great earth shook, the sentient beings who were being transformed were struck with fear, their hair standing on end."
Ānanda replied: “So it is, Blessed One;
so it is, Sugata. I have now seen this youth, who has come through the air, manifesting various displays of supernatural power.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"A palanquin such as this, adorned with various interspersed jewels, approaches before the youth, emitting all manner of diverse and wondrous fragrances that fill this buddha-field."
Ānanda replied: “So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"This matter is manifested through the power of that good man’s wisdom, enabling this carriage to emit such wondrous fragrance.
Ānanda! Listen further:
it can also produce four kinds of sounds—namely, the sound of emptiness, the sound of non-existence, the sound of tranquility, and the sound of the Buddha."
Ānanda replied, “So be it,
Blessed One. The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"Furthermore, from the pores of the youth, such sounds as these issued forth. Ānanda!

When these sounds issued forth, sixty-eight nayutas of sentient beings attained great benefit; moreover, among the multitude of sentient beings in a thousand worlds, many beings, through the unconditioned dharma, had their mental outflows forever exhausted and thereby attained liberation."

Ānanda! Having heard the name of a single Buddha, nine hundred million bodhisattvas have already dwelled in the stage of non-retrogression and attained entry into the noble path toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In this realm, within the world of humans and devas, two hundred thousand nayutas of devas and humans attained the stage of non-retrogression and became firmly established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Ānanda! To the west of where this son of good family resides, there is a Buddha named Prāmodyaruta, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. His world is named Lomaharṣaṇī. He has come from that land desiring to see the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa."
This son of good family, having already arrived, has brought great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings. Ānanda!
Now, when this son of good family comes to this land, he performs great Buddha-work; just as the Tathāgata turns the Great Wheel of Dharma, so too does he turn the Great Wheel of Dharma.

Ānanda! Since incalculable eons past, this son of good family has constantly emitted these four kinds of sounds—from his pores—namely, sounds such as "emptiness" and "quiescence. Within each and every sound, he brings great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What roots of goodness did this son of good family cultivate in the past, such that he is now able to produce these various sounds from all his pores?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"I recall that in the past, immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Vimalanetra (Stainless Eye), a Sugata, a Knower of the World, an Unsurpassed One, a Tamer of Men, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One."
This son of good family went forth in the presence of that Buddha, becoming a great śramaṇa named Jñānarata, and purely cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
That śramaṇa questioned that Tathāgata regarding the True Principle, wisdom that is difficult to know, and the meaning of the most profound phrases—namely, non-arising and non-ceasing;
that all phenomena are empty and non-existent; that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is quiescent; and that all Buddhas are of one and the same essence.

For seven days and seven nights, that śramaṇa continued without interruption, without thinking of fatigue, without thinking of other matters, and without laying down his heavy burden; he personally received and upheld these four phrases, thoroughly savoring them through recitation, skillfully maintaining them until they were mastered, wisely penetrating their meaning, and refining his own practice with diligent application.
“Ānanda! The śramaṇa at that time was this very boy.

By means of these four lines of sublime meaning—which have been spoken together by billions of Buddhas—he entered the teachings of all Buddhas, gathered in all sentient beings, and furthermore spontaneously attained the realization of awakening.”
That śramaṇa, out of compassion for all sentient beings, traveled among villages, hamlets, towns, and cities to preach the Dharma to them.

"Ānanda! At that time, the Dharma-preacher Śramaṇa Jñānarata, through his extensive learning, understood the meaning and intent of the Dharma; furthermore, with a sincere heart, he proclaimed these verses of the Dharma for others for six years."
By these causes and conditions, for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), such sounds of supernormal power (*abhijñā*) have issued from all his pores.
For this reason, this good man issues these four kinds of Dharma-sounds from the pores of his body, bringing great benefit to many sentient beings.
In this successive manner, throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), this youth has perfected these four kinds of sublime voices within the pores of his body. "Ānanda!..."

The people of Jambudvīpa have attained great and excellent benefit, they have attained the foremost benefit, if they even hear the name of this Bodhisattva Apratiṣṭhita; how much more so if they hear his Dharma?

Ānanda! If there are good men or good women, whether in the heavens or among humans, who hear even the name of this Bodhisattva Without-Object-of-Attachment, they will attain a pure mind; the merit they obtain is inconceivable, let alone those who gaze upon, behold, or meet him face-to-face.
Why is this so? Ānanda! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Apratiṣṭhita has already attained inconceivable and ineffable merits within the various bodhisattva stages.
Ānanda! It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to come and see the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa. Ānanda!
"You should now prepare a seat for that great bodhisattva before the Tathāgata, intended for this son of good family to sit upon.
Ānanda! You shall obtain great peace, happiness, and benefit, and you shall also swiftly attain supreme and wondrous supernatural powers."

Ānanda! Because of the karmic causes and conditions of having prepared this matting, the fruit and retribution you shall obtain will be such that whether sitting or lying down, you will always enjoy peace and stability; and within a single moment of thought, you shall directly realize the unconditioned noble Dharma of the fruit of Arhatship.

Ānanda! For you who have not yet realized the fruit of an untainted Śrāvaka saint, I now bestow upon you the prediction that you shall attain it; furthermore, you shall possess portions of various merits which you should dedicate toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and you shall thereby attain the great Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.

“Ānanda! If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās; or gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and other sentient beings, who hear this prophecy spoken by Śāntamati, and having heard it, attain a pure and profound mind as well as faith and understanding;”

Furthermore, if there is anyone who wishes to hear this Dharma-gate of the prophecy of the Silent Teaching—whether hearing it from the Tathāgata or from a śrāvaka—and moreover prepares a seat for that Dharma-master, the merit they obtain will be no different from that of the Dharma-master sitting upon this seat and preaching this Dharma-gate of the prophecy of the Silent Teaching.
Why is that? Ānanda! Having prepared the seat, that person shall obtain ten kinds of merit from such preparation.
What are the ten? First, one shall obtain the seat of a universal monarch (cakravartin); second, the seat of Śakra;
third, the seat of Brahmā; fourth, the seat of a world-ruler; fifth, the seat of the world...

The world [attains] the seat of a Dharma-preacher from all Buddhas; sixth, having fulfilled the bodhisattva stages and attained that rank, one sits upon the high lotus lion-throne beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment;
seventh, having realized all-knowledge, one attains unsurpassed bodhi and sits upon the Buddha-seat; eighth, ...
Ninth, when turning the great wheel of Dharma, one obtains the throne for turning the wheel of Dharma, adorned by immeasurable billions of devas; tenth,
when wishing to manifest great supernormal powers, one transcends all worldly paths to obtain the lion throne of supreme manifestation, the greatest supernormal power of the Tathāgata.
When he desired to manifest entry into Great Parinirvāṇa, he attained the state of a Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, causing the minds of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans to be inspired.
Rejoicing, they attain pure faith; finally, all conditioned phenomena are extinguished, and they abide in the vajra-samādhi, attaining the seat of the Tathāgata. Ānanda!
"You shall obtain these ten kinds of rewards for the lion throne. Ānanda!

If there are good men or good women who, with a pure mind, hear the meaning of these verses from the *Dharmaparyāya of the Silent Proclamation of the Prediction*, and because they desire, revere, and respect that Dharma-preacher, they arrange a Dharma seat for him—by this causal condition, they shall each achieve the rewards of these ten kinds of lion thrones."
For this reason, Ānanda!

You should join your palms in reverence toward the Bodhisattva Aśraya-pariśuddha; you shall thereby obtain great benefit, peace, and happiness, as well as a great mass of merit. By virtue of this merit, you will swiftly attain the development of supernatural powers (ṛddhi).

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having prepared the Dharma seat for the young man Niśraya-apratiṣṭhita, joined his palms toward the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Niśraya-apratiṣṭhita, giving rise to a mind of pure faith, a mind of reverence, and a mind of shame and modesty; he then spoke these verses at that moment:
"Joining my palms toward this hero, Who has subdued the dragon and entered meditative absorption— The great wise king of the assembly, The radiance of Niśraya-apratiṣṭhita."
"Having attained wisdom and diligence, The aggregate of wisdom and meditative concentration,
Peerless in the world, I join my palms toward the Fearless One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda in verse:
“Now that you respectfully join your palms in homage and make offerings without attachment,
I shall explain for you the various fruits and rewards you will obtain.
Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, after my parinirvāṇa...”
In village dwellings and settlements, among my disciples,
whether entering a village or departing from that village,
and in all modes of conduct— walking, standing, sitting, or lying down— [I am always present].
You shall perform a great Buddhist service. All manner of beings, whether sentient or insentient,
shall all turn toward you, bowing their bodies in reverent homage.

"Whether they be men or women, male devas or female devas, or various non-Buddhists such as the Pārivrajakas; whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kings, ministers, state preceptors, military generals, or other officials and subordinates; whether they be elders, householders, or any other ordinary beings possessing form—even down to the six domestic animals, elephants, horses, running beasts, and all winged birds—if they see you, they shall all attain pure faith.
Furthermore, all trees, medicinal herbs, crops, flowers, and fruits shall all bow their bodies toward you in reverent homage."

All the terraces, palaces, houses, multi-storied pavilions, watchtowers, battlements, loopholes, vehicles, and litters—all were eclipsed by the power of your merit and majestic radiance; they all bowed their bodies toward you in this manner.

“Ānanda! For example, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha first realizes anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and attains unimpeded liberation, all crops, trees, medicinal herbs, and various flowers and fruits—even briefly speaking, including humans and non-humans—completely fill the bodhimaṇḍa and all bow their bodies toward the Tathāgata in reverent homage.”
Ānanda! It is so, it is so.

Because of the power of this present cause and condition—your joining of palms and bowing of the body before this son of good family who is free from攀緣 (parāmarśa)—in all future postures and wherever you may be, humans and non-humans alike, as well as all crops, trees, and medicinal herbs, shall all bow their bodies in reverence toward you.

“Ānanda! If there be sons or daughters of good family who, either after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata or during my own present lifetime, should for even a moment hear this Dharma-text of the prediction of adornment; or even if they join their ten fingers in palms-together gesture for a single thought-moment, or through the causal conditions of a single thought, or with a sincere heart contemplate this meaning and give rise to a single act of faith—such a person shall obtain a reward of merit as I have previously described.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!

In future ages, there will be few sentient beings who hear this Dharma; indeed, they will be even fewer than those who merely hear the name of such a fundamental teaching. Even hearing it once or twice is difficult to attain, let alone hearing it and then attaining true faith, revering and honoring it, refraining from slander, eliminating doubt, contemplating and practicing it, and giving rise to the perception of its reality.

Regarding such sons and daughters of good family, I see them all with my Buddha-eye and I know them all with my Buddha-wisdom; such persons as these have not practiced or made offerings under only one Buddha, nor have they planted roots of goodness under only one Buddha.

"Ānanda! Now, this entire assembly gathered before me—these multitudes of devas and humans, men and women—have come specifically because they wish to see the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, enter parinirvāṇa."
