Ānanda! When Maitreya Bodhisattva first attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a future age—after he has received the rank of wisdom and until he sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)—this assembly shall offer great offerings, honoring and revering him with respect.

In this successive manner, until the time when the World-Honored One Maitreya enters parinirvāṇa, they shall likewise observe; at that very time, remaining by the side of the Tathāgata, they shall again behold these four youths listening to the Dharma in such a way.

Now, having previously been able to see and hear this son of good family, Non-Appropriation (Apratiṣṭhita), who within a single pore hears the vast and subtle sounds of the Great Dharma, I have experienced great joy upon hearing those sounds.
Therefore, Ānanda! Now that you have heard such subtle and profound meanings being taught, you should repeatedly bow your body, join your palms, and maintain a pure mind of reverent faith.

Why is this so? Because by means of such a pure mind and reverent faith in the causes and conditions of wholesome karma, wherever you may be, all sentient beings, devas, and people of the world will revere, make offerings to, respect, and praise you; they will bow their bodies before you, and even after your parinirvāṇa, devas and people of the world will erect stupas to make offerings to your relics.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aniruddha, saying: "Aniruddha!
You see those forty billion devas and humans in the upper realms who, having heard this sutra, all stand with palms joined and bodies bowed."
Aniruddha replied to the Buddha,
“So it is, Blessed One. The Buddha spoke again to Aniruddha:

“Because those devas and humans have heard this Dharma, they join their palms with faith and bow their bodies; by these roots of goodness, for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in future ages, they shall not fall into the evil realms. Whether in the heavens or among humans, after passing through births throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin rājā*). In every place of birth, they shall constantly encounter the Buddhas and, in the presence of those Buddhas, accomplish roots of goodness.”

Having perfected their roots of goodness, they shall eventually realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, all bearing the same name: Sarvasattvāvanata-kāya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

When these words had been spoken, there were among the great assembly various *malla* warriors and their retinues, each numbering five hundred. Their names were: the Warrior Amusing, the Warrior Head-Kuṇapa, the Warrior Great Strength, the Warrior Celestial Power, the Warrior Surpassing Gods, the Warrior Ugra, the Warrior Fearless, the Warrior Vasu, the Warrior Truth, the Warrior Uttara, the Warrior Vāhu, and the Warrior All-Enduring. Each of these warriors, together with his retinue of five hundred, gathered and assembled at the head of the multitude. Desiring to make offerings, they approached the place where the Tathāgata was; all with bodies half-bowed, palms joined, weeping piteously, crying out with choked voices, and tears streaming down their faces like rain, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We now, desiring to make offerings to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, as well as to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Aśvayujaputra, and to the other immeasurable great Bodhisattvas, even unto all the venerable Śrāvakas—for the sake of making offerings to this subtle and profound meaning of the sūtra, this pure dharma-gate—we join our palms and bow our bodies.
“World-Honored One!
By means of these roots of goodness from this single thought-moment, we dedicate them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately smiled.

It is the natural law of all Buddhas that when they smile, various subtle and wondrous rays of light of diverse colors—namely blue, yellow, red, white, gold, and crystal—issue forth from their mouths. Having emitted these rays, they pervade immeasurable and boundless worlds; the illumination reaches as far as the Brahma palaces, then returns to circumambulate the World-Honored One three times before entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having witnessed this event, addressed the Buddha in verse:
"For what cause does the Lamp of the World emit Such a great radiance?"
“Excellent! Resolve my doubts, as well as those of other sentient beings.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Did you see it?”

This son of a Malla, with a single-minded focus, joined his palms toward me and the Bodhisattva Aśvapratibaddha; he conceived sincere and pure faith in this sutra and further resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.
Ānanda replied, “I have seen them, World-Honored One!
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"This son of a Malla shall, from this day forward, not fall into the evil realms for incalculable billions of kalpas; thereafter, he will realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: “Ānanda!
Do you not see how the sons of Māra have gathered together, their hearts filled with great joy, bowing their bodies toward me?”
Speaking these words with joy, they shall attain the unsurpassed path.
These sons of the Greatly Wise One have made offerings to me and to the Non-referential; they have conceived reverence for the Dharma.
All my śrāvakas, having thus joined their palms,
shall not fall into the evil realms for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
By virtue of this karma of joining palms and bowing toward me, they shall attain liberation.
Even if one were to speak for an eon, or for countless billions of eons,
these ones shall realize the Way and bring all Buddha-lands to fulfillment.
They practice the most supreme conduct, their number being immeasurable.
Even through kalpas numbering in the hundreds of millions, one could not know it by means of thought. Ānanda!
Now, before long, in this very last watch of the night, I shall part from you; this is our final meeting.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda: "Ānanda!
Do you see that great golden light shining forth coming from the north?"

His majestic radiance eclipsed all else; the trees, crops, medicinal herbs, flowers, and fruits, as well as the mountain cliffs, mounds, terraces, palaces, towers, litters, carriages, and all beings—human and non-human—in that region, together with the space above them, all became a single color, namely, the color of gold.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
“So it is, Blessed One. The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"Do you see that from the north there further come seven palanquins made of Jambūnada gold?
In the central palanquin, a youth sits cross-legged; his majestic radiance is most supreme, and his merit is towering and sublime."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So it is, Bhagavān; I have now seen it.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"To the north, sixty-four hundred thousand *koṭis* of worlds away from this buddha-field, there is a buddha-field named Kusumāvati (Sui: Duohua, 'Abounding in Flowers')."
In that land, the World-Honored One is named Bodhipakṣaparivarta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Within that buddha-field, there was this youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Puṣpavyūhābhijñāguṇa, who cast off his body from there and was reborn in this land.
“Ānanda! In that world, the sound of all dharmas issues forth, called the ‘Sound of the Factors of Enlightenment.
Any sentient beings there who hear this sound will bring all roots of goodness to fulfillment.”
Ānanda! That Tathāgata Pravartabodhipakṣa has been teaching the Dharma in the present for sixty-four thousand kalpas since he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Ānanda! That Tathāgata has no assembly of śrāvakas; he has only an assembly of bodhisattvas. Ānanda!
For example, a consecrated universal monarch (cakravartin) has many sons, who serve as his ministers, state preceptors, or minor kings;
in this very same way, the bodhisattvas of that Buddha-Tathāgata are likewise so, being called both "sons" and "ministers," and that Buddha is also like that.
There are two bodhisattvas who are most preeminent, serving as the sole attendants among all bodhisattvas; they take bodhisattvas themselves as the Jewel of the Saṅgha. Ānanda!
In this manner, he spoke in succession regarding those buddha-fields, all of which were entirely filled with bodhisattvas. "Ānanda!
In that buddha-world, all necessities of life are abundant and sufficient, lacking nothing whatsoever."
Endowed with fearlessness, peace, and happiness, it is subtle and wondrous, filled with people worthy of being beheld; the merits of the Bodhisattva are all fully perfected.
Abiding in the various supernormal powers, he is most preeminent; through the power of samādhi, he moves to and fro.
Like a friend who is a mass of wisdom, he is most preeminent, his treasury of knowledge being fully satisfied.

They are always able to cultivate the bodhicitta and always able to discourse upon the teachings of omniscience; regarding all the profound dharmas of the bodhisattvas, they have fully realized them in their infinite and boundless extent.
Ānanda! Such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these fill that world.
Among those buddha-fields, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva—the noble son Puṣpadāna-ṛddhiguṇa—has come to be born here in Jambudvīpa, in the city of Vaiśālī.

That son of good family has now manifested supernatural powers and come here because he wishes to prostrate at the feet of the Tathāgata and also desires to behold the World-Honored One entering great parinirvāṇa.
“Ānanda! This manifestation of great radiance is due to the majestic spiritual power of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

Ānanda! These seven palanquins made of Jambūnada gold were manifested as a transformation because they represent the seven factors of enlightenment, which are the auxiliary dharmas for the path of that Tathāgata.

“Ānanda! In this Jambudvīpa, there are immeasurable thousands of koṭis of sentient beings, including devas and humans, who have together with this youth planted roots of goodness since the distant past.

When this youth was born here in Jambudvīpa, he caused those sentient beings to immediately attain immeasurable joy and exultation. Furthermore, some sentient beings were to attain the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya); some were to attain the stage of learning (śaikṣabhūmi); some were to attain the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣabhūmi); some sentient beings who had not yet resolved upon bodhicitta were to be inspired to generate that mind; and some sentient beings were to give rise to the innate, non-retrogressive mind of patience (kṣānti).”

“Ānanda! As for this light emitted by this youth who sits cross-legged within the central palanquin—it is the manifestation of the supernatural power and majesty of that Tathāgata; from this light, those six palanquins have emerged.”
Ānanda! Behold!

By the majestic spiritual power of that Tathāgata, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Puṣpadrumakūṭa-vikrānta-guṇarāja is able to manifest various supernatural powers in this place; furthermore, by the power of this radiance, he is able to bring great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings in this world, namely, by mutually sustaining them through that True Dharma.

At that time, those youths all gathered together in harmony, leaping for joy with great exultation; surrounded by hundreds of thousands of beings before and behind them, they rained down various kinds of flowers in a single kṣaṇa and proceeded toward the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda!
That which the Tathāgata must perform for all sentient beings, and that which the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—the eldest sons of the Tathāgata—must perform, I have now fully accomplished;
the benefit for sentient beings that I was to provide has now been completed.
Ānanda! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Puṣpavyūha-ṛddhiguṇa sits majestically within a carriage of Jāmbūnada gold;
by means of such miraculous powers as these, he transforms and guides nayutas of beings.
He personally realized the fruit of arhatship and further taught a number of beings equal to ten million nayutas so that they attained the stage of those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Furthermore, he caused a hundred koṭis of beings to develop pure faith in the Triple Gem and receive and uphold the five precepts;
additionally, he enabled seven hundred koṭis of devas to abide in the state of non-retrogression.
He will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; furthermore,
he will cause seven koṭis of sentient beings to abide in the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and he will cause immeasurable,
asaṃkhyeya, nayuta-koṭis of sentient beings to encounter the first assembly of the World-Honored One Maitreya.
The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Four Youthful Boys, Middle Fascicle;
The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Four Youthful Boys, Lower Fascicle.
Translated during the Sui Dynasty by [the monk from] Gandhāra in North India.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that the World-Honored One will remain for a full kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa, out of compassion for these sentient beings. Why is this?

If the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha remains in the world, such great matters as these will constantly manifest in the world, and it will cause these truly virtuous mahāsattvas to repeatedly travel back and forth within Jambudvīpa.
We sentient beings, moreover, should for this much time behold these great assemblies of bodhisattvas performing services and making offerings;
furthermore, at this time, such sutras as these should be widely propagated and disseminated;
and for this much time, we shall hear the teachings that accord with the meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
For such a length of time, we have been granted the opportunity to behold the various manifestations of supernatural power by the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, and the Great Beings.

If the Tathāgata were not to remain in the world today but were instead to enter parinirvāṇa, we sentient beings would be deprived of three things after the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has passed away.
What are these three? They are:
not seeing the Buddha; not hearing the True Dharma; and thirdly, not seeing the vast and expansive mind of such Great Beings, nor being able to attend upon or make offerings to them.
Such are the losses incurred.

After the Venerable Ānanda had spoken these words, he wailed and wept bitterly; filled with grief, sighing and distressed, his eyes brimming with tears, he rolled upon the ground like a felled tree, crying out:
"We have been swiftly separated from the Buddha; we are also separated from our spiritual friends."
At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Kalyāṇārthacintin, who addressed the venerable Ānanda in verse:
“Ānanda, do not be distressed; All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
If one desires for worldly dharmas to be permanent, Such a thing is impossible to find.”
If one says that there are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), such a statement cannot be established.
Since all these dharmas are empty, why do you now suffer in grief?
All forms of knowledge are entirely empty; even the Buddha’s wisdom is empty.
Since even a Buddha cannot be apprehended, why do you now grieve and sorrow?
Do not give rise to conceptual discrimination; the wise abandon discrimination.
All phenomena are like space, like a mirage appearing as water.
Just as a magician conjures illusions— elephants, horses, various vehicles,
gardens, villages, trees, and all manner of flowers and fruits—
so too is the conventional truth; like a magical transformation, it lacks any reality.
“The Buddhas and their śrāvakas are likewise thus, no different.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Bodhisattva Bhadramatin with these verses:
“It is just as you have said; all dharmas are without marks.”
"This is the most supreme Dharma, which I have now heard for the last time.
How shall I proceed toward Śrāvastī? To what question shall I give my reply? "Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
Where is the Buddha?
When will the Eye of the World come?
In the past, when I went to that place, I constantly beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"Now that he has gone to that empty place, where shall I, of great wisdom, dwell?
Then, the young man Śāntivṛtti again addressed the Venerable Ānanda in verse, saying:
"Even if you wept for a hundred million years, this matter would still be difficult to attain."
Ānanda! Observe closely this place within the Dharma-realm that is difficult to see:
it is like the trunk of a plantain tree; when every leaf is peeled away, [nothing remains].
In between there is no reality; the nature of phenomena is likewise so.
Just as when the heavens send down rain, droplets of water fall everywhere, bubbles arise and then vanish; so too it is with all conditioned things.
Like a mass of water bubbles, which those with eyes behold,
yet in this place there is no reality— so too are the characteristics of the world.
Like a reflection in a mirror, its substance has no reality.
"The phenomena of the three realms are thus; O wise one, do not weep.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śāntamati in verse:
"I am not unaware of this, as you, a wise one, have said."
The Great Sage has declared in the sutras that all three marks are impermanent.
Yet these billions of devas weep and wail, crying out toward me; because of this, suffering arises within me.
Before long the World-Honored One will depart, leaving behind our eyes;
where shall we turn? Who can protect us?
From whom did you hear the True Dharma, so tranquil and incomparably deep?
To whom do I now offer my worship? Alas!
“The Buddha is difficult to behold!
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Apratiṣṭhita addressed the Venerable Ānanda in verse, saying:
“Venerable Ānanda, arise! Observe only the Dharma and do not grieve.”
Dharmas have no one who comes, nor do they have anyone who goes.
Just as the Buddha has birth, so too is the realization of bodhi;
just as there is the turning of the wheel of Dharma, so too is nirvāṇa.
The Buddhas have never been born, Nor have they ever ceased to exist.
Within suchness, the true Dharma, Ānanda, why do you weep?
You hear from my pores These various sounds emerging.
"All things are empty and quiescent; these are the four matters concerning the Buddhas.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Anālambana in verse, saying:
"Great Beings such as yourselves will, before long, each depart for separate lands."
In that land you shall see the Buddhas preaching the Dharma of ambrosia.
Having heard that Buddha’s teaching and its most profound and wondrous meanings,
you shall behold his assembly of disciples as well as the various bodhisattvas.
Now we, the gods numbering in the hundreds of millions, surround you in weeping;
since the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, where shall the Wise One dwell?
O thousands of upāsakas, listen to me today!
Greatly afflicted by suffering, grief, and lamentation, how can I console you?
May the gods of the Thirty-three, Yama, Tuṣita, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin,
as well as the gods of the Brahma heavens— may such deities as these come.
How can they be made to rejoice?
After the Bull among Men has passed away, how shall his Dharma be proclaimed?
How shall my mouth possess such eloquence?
The devas asked me: "Ānanda! Where is the Venerable One?"
When he asked me what my reply was, I said:
"The Tathāgata dwells in all places in a most profound manner;
as for me, in this forest where I practice walking meditation, where exactly am I now?"
At that time, the son of good family, Puṣpaphala-ṛddhiguṇa, addressed the Venerable Ānanda in verse:
"I know your conduct; during these three months, I have frequently manifested my form before you. Ānanda, do not weep."
For the sake of you, I have told of the remaining thousands of Buddhas;
all those Buddhas have spoken for you, manifesting themselves in the form of the Śākya clan.
All Buddhas possess compassionate thoughts, for you have a fondness for honoring the Buddhas.
He is coming toward you; Ānanda, do not weep aloud.
Today all the worlds, including the gods, have cause for grief and sorrow, for such a Great Teacher has vanished into stillness and is no longer manifest.
"The Tathāgata once spoke of his lifespan abiding for a hundred million eons;
yet all conditioned phenomena perish moment by moment—this I heard from my Teacher.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda stood behind the Buddha and, with three great cries, spoke this verse:
"The one to whom sentient beings turn for refuge, who could grant them the eye—
after the Guide has entered parinirvāṇa, sentient beings will become blind and dark.
Upon hearing these unwholesome words, King Ajātaśatru,"
After the Guide has entered parinirvāṇa, how shall we dwell amidst sorrow and suffering?
Now that the Supreme Person has attained nirvāṇa,
the son of the Mallas and others like him will experience such grief and affliction, wailing and weeping aloud.
Having gathered together, they finally beheld the Teacher;
with hearts full of reverence, they paid him honor, joining their palms and bowing low.
Devas, nāgas, and yakṣas filled the area for five yojanas in length and breadth.
There is no vacancy here; there is no place for humans to enter.
A rain of subtle, fragrant flowers falls, filling the ground up to the knees;
furthermore, a rain of various powdered incenses falls as an offering to the Supreme Sage.
Nanda and Upananda, along with six billion nāgas,
all came to the place of parinirvāṇa to see the Teacher for the last time.
Mānasvin, Varuṇa, Sāgara, and the great nāgas—
Ghoru and Mucilinda, each surrounded by ten billion followers,
raised clouds and rains of fragrant water, sprinkling this great earth;
descending with a great downpour, they finally beheld the Teacher.
The various devas rained down celestial flowers and showered pure fragrant water;
the devas, nāgas, and others, with hearts full of reverence, made offerings to the World-Honored One.
The Nāga King Anavatapta and sixty koṭis of others likewise did so.
A rain of various jewels fell, reaching the presence of the Human Bull-King (the Buddha).
Elāpattra wept; the great serpent, son of Sumeru, for the sake of making offerings to the World-Honored One, was the last to behold the Buddha.
Hundreds of thousands of nāgas, numbering in the billions and nayutas,
raised clouds and shook thunder and lightning;
they came to where the Teacher was and poured down a great rain of pure, fragrant waters.
Furthermore, for the sake of making offerings, thousands of millions of yakṣas, or hundreds of nayutas, all come desiring to see the Buddha,
recollecting the various merits of the Buddha as they behold the World-Honored One for the last time.
Furthermore, the Four Heavenly Kings, their faces filled with tears of sorrow,
came to the side of the Teacher to behold the Buddha for the last time.
Śakra Devānām Indra, surrounded by the hosts of devas, [did likewise].
Sixty-three thousand in number have already arrived at the Buddha’s abode;
they rain down celestial flowers, exquisite māndārava blossoms,
and sandalwood powder, making offerings to the Supreme Sage.
The Brahmā Viśvabhu with his topknot, surrounded by a host of two Brahmās,
wept as he approached the Buddha’s dwelling, seeing the Tathāgata for the last time.
By the majestic power of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, many hundreds of billions of devas [gathered].
Wailing and weeping, they went to where the Buddha was, for the Buddha was now entering nirvana.
Countless billions of devas, each mourning in various ways,
entreated the Great Teacher, praying that he would remain for one kalpa.
The son of Māra, of great wisdom, named Satavāha,
arrived sorrowfully at the place where the Buddha was, because the Supreme Sage was about to enter nirvāṇa.
He clasped the feet of the World-Honored One and, bowing his body, entreated the Buddha.
Out of compassion for the world, O King of Śākyas, may you remain for one kalpa.
If the World-Honored One should remain, it will bring inconceivable benefit to the great benevolent devas; we entreat the Honored One to remain for one kalpa.
At that time, the noble son Apratiṣṭhita addressed all those devas, worldlings, Brahmā kings, merchant lords, and sons of Māra with these verses:
"You do not all understand: This child is like a monkey;
His mind is constantly dissipated— Why does he wail and weep?"
Just as a pig, while sleeping, suddenly awakens and loses its composure,
When being butchered with knives and flayed, it flees in terror and runs away;
Such is the vision of my mind, and such is the state of you all.
Those who in the past did not hear the Dharma did so because of greed and negligence.
Today, the torch of wisdom is about to be extinguished and no longer appear;
while the Buddha is still present, you should perform virtuous deeds.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, Pūrṇa, Subhūti, as well as the youth Rājaputra Amoghadarśin, the Elder Kāśyapa, Mahākauṣṭhila, and all the other elders:
"I now say to you, O bhikṣus: bring me your right hands."
When those bhikṣus had heard these words from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they immediately addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
At that time, one thousand bhikṣus gathered together, each offering his right hand to the World-Honored One.
Then, the World-Honored One took hold of the right hands of all those bhikṣus with his left hand.
Having taken hold of them, he again took the hands of Rāhula and Ānanda with his right hand, placed them into the hands of the bhikṣus, and gave this final instruction: "You, bhikṣus!..."
"I, Ānanda the Worthy, and the Elder Rāhula, now entrust you and bequeath our charge to you.
At that moment, they let out a great cry; such a cry of lamentation and weeping shook heaven and earth in a most terrifying manner, and that great sound pervaded this entire Buddha-field.
At that time, when Rāhula and Ānanda were being entrusted with the teachings, five hundred bhikṣus in the assembly, having witnessed this event, immediately cast off their bodies and lives.
Why is this? Those bhikṣus could not bear to see the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa; they thought to themselves: "It would be better for us to enter nirvāṇa first.

We cannot bear to see this Great Lamp of the World, the Guide of the World, the Great Compassionate Father, the Supreme Good Friend, who has pity on sentient beings and constantly bestows worldly happiness, now enter into extinction—how could we bear to witness it?"
At that moment, during that kṣaṇa, lava, and muhūrta, five hundred buddhas, each residing in their own land, all extended their right hands to Śākyamuni.
At that time, the World-Honored One again took the hands of Ānanda and the elder Rāhula with his own hand and entrusted them into the hands of those Tathāgatas, speaking these verses:
"This is my son Rāhula, And Ānanda is my attendant;
Now before all the Buddhas, I entrust these two to you."
In the latter part of this very night, I shall enter parinirvāṇa;
you shall no longer see me.
There will be no refuge, no protector, and no one to show compassion.
Except for the various World-Honored Ones, who conceal their inconceivable compassion;
as I observe all the worlds, they are inconceivable and immeasurable—
I do not see a single sentient being— so for whose sake do I now abide?
For immeasurable thousands of kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
I have dwelt for the sake of even a single sentient being throughout such kalpas.
Having already benefited those sentient beings who possess faith and a reverent mind,
"The rest, who lack faith, even billions of Buddhas could not transform.
At that time, five hundred Buddhas spoke in unison with one voice, reciting these verses:
"The Honored One has already benefited sentient beings; the Honored One has completed the work of a Buddha."
Manifesting various supernatural powers, he has finished beating the great Dharma drum.
Having sufficed for billions of sentient beings like rain from clouds moistening the earth,
the Great Seer of the Śākya clan has extracted the poisonous arrows from sentient beings.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda and the Venerable Rāhula knelt with both knees upon the ground and addressed those Buddhas in verse, saying:
"Great Beings, we entreat you: May the Honored Ones remain for one kalpa."
By the power of the Buddha, all who possess the eye of vision behold the Most Victorious One among two-legged beings; because the One of Great Wisdom dwells in the world,
many sentient beings have faith and obtain inconceivable benefit.
"The various devas and humans increase, while the asuras decrease;
śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are born in great numbers beyond conception.
At that time, those five hundred buddhas addressed the Venerable Ānanda and Rāhula, saying:
“O sons of good family! Do not weep excessively;
do not grieve excessively. Such is the nature of things;
such is the exhaustion of phenomena; such is reality; such are all conditioned formations (saṃskāra).”
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), all constructed phenomena (*kṛtaka-dharma*), and all conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are entirely like this.
Such is the ultimate limit; having already relinquished body and life, the practice of the Tathāgata is immeasurable. Because conventional truths are thus, one cannot attain mastery.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, not a conditioned body; he does not abide in worldly dharmas, so you should not request that the Tathāgata remain.
O sons of good family!

"Cease for a moment, all of you; once you have reached my Buddha-field, Śākyamuni Tathāgata will immediately extend his right hand and emit a radiance, and that radiance shall illuminate my buddha-land."
Having illuminated that land, you shall return and see Śākyamuni Buddha before you, preaching the Dharma for you and enabling you to hear it.
Therefore, do not grieve excessively.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered into samādhi.

Having dwelt in samādhi, he immediately extended his right hand; from the palm of that hand down to the tip of the thumb, as well as from all the joints of his body, down to the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on his feet, and within the marks of the soft, webbed hands and feet, from his copper-colored nails to the spaces between his ten fingers and the precious lines of his palms, he emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light.

From each and every ray of light, hundreds of thousands of billions of lotuses are miraculously produced; from each and every lotus pedestal, hundreds of thousands of billions of miraculous lion thrones are manifested; upon each and every throne, one Buddha is seen seated; and each and every manifested Buddha teaches and transforms immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings—some among them attaining the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), others attaining the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāgabhūmi*). All such phenomena produced by the rays of light emitted from all these marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) are likewise identical.
This is also the case for the area between the navel and the private organ (*kośagatavastiguhyatā*); it is likewise so for the area between the eyebrows on the face.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted hundreds of thousands of kinds of light rays from the crown of his head; at the tip of each light ray, he manifested hundreds of billions of lotus flowers, and upon each flower pedestal, he transformed hundreds of billions of lion thrones, and upon each throne, he manifested a Buddha seated there to preach the wondrous Dharma.

Those Tathāgatas do not teach any other dharmas; they teach only the Bodhisattva Guhyakośa Sūtra and various dhāraṇīs and vajra-phrase chapters, clearly explaining for others such dharma-gates as the purity of the three spheres, the powers, and the fearlessnesses of the Tathāgatas.

Each of these emanated Buddhas preached the Dharma, able to purify immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them to abide in the stage of non-retrogression and turn toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was lying on his right side upon the lion’s couch between the twin śāla trees, he manifested a transformed Buddha lying on his right side.
Having completed this manifestation, his own body immediately traveled to the Saṃjīva Great Hell.
Having arrived there, his body emitted a radiance.
Once the radiance was emitted, its light shone everywhere throughout the Saṃjīva Hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having illuminated the great Saṃjīva Hell with this radiance, spoke these verses:
"These sentient beings die again and again, and repeatedly return to life;
yet they do not abandon those perceptions, and thus give rise to all manner of suffering and affliction.
When a Sage appears in this world, the World-Honored One is able to create illumination."
One who can expound all the true dharmas extinguishes all suffering and affliction.
Unconditioned and inexhaustible, without cessation and without activity—
if one can understand it thus, they shall not fall into the various realms of existence.

At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, within that very kṣaṇa, lava, and muhūrta, he caused those thirty billion suffering beings in the Great Reviving Hell to cast off their bodies.
Immediately after casting off his body, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At that time, the World-Honored One again went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and recited these verses; by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the sound pervaded all the great hells.

Those immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings in the hell realm, having cast off their hellish bodies, were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; once reborn as devas, they again recollected the Dharma previously taught and all attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
At that time, having attained the fruit of the Dharma, the sons of the gods realized the Dharma and realized the fruit; entering into all phenomena, they spoke these verses together:
"Just as on a vast wilderness road, There is a wise merchant leader Who delivers many sentient beings From those who are plundered by bandits and beasts."
The World-Honored One is likewise so, the unsurpassed Great Caravan Leader,
who can deliver billions of sentient beings bound within birth and death.
We take refuge in the Buddha, the Radiant Great Caravan Leader.
Arising compassion for us, you are able to liberate us from all suffering and affliction;
we take refuge in the Dharma, which our own bodies have realized;
we take refuge in the Saṅgha, whose merit is inconceivable.
At that time, the World-Honored One shone his cool and refreshing light universally upon the Avīci (A-bi-zhi) Hell.

Having created this coolness—he extinguished all the heat, afflictions, and poisonous sufferings, accomplished thousands of billions of portions of all dharmas, enabled all to attain various joys and pleasures, and compassionately moistened and benefited all sentient beings—comforting, softening, pitying, and bringing joy, benefit, and peace to them; he conjoined the three gates of emptiness: signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*)—and addressed those sentient beings in hell, speaking these verses:
“Emptiness and signlessness, Non-arising and non-ceasing...”
"If one understands such a Dharma as this, one shall be liberated from the evil realms.

At that time, eight hundred thousand *koṭis* of sentient beings heard these verses. What was spoken in these verses was unimpeded throughout the three periods of time; these various dharmas were divided into hundreds of thousands of kinds, reaching their ears pure and sublime.
Having heard this sound, they cast off their hellish bodies from the Great Hell of Avīci and were immediately reborn in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
At that time, the World-Honored One, residing in the Brahma Palace, further spoke these verses:
“The supreme happiness of sentient beings Is to be free from all places of suffering;”
The locus where names and signs are spoken, as well as all inverted perceptions—
these the hero should abandon, and thus he shall be freed from all suffering and affliction.
All such perceptions are inverted, as is attachment to the perception of what is not form.
What joy is there in the three realms?
One wanders through birth again and again; having died, one is born once more, increasing and perpetuating suffering.
One who can know emptiness through wisdom likewise does not cling to emptiness.
That person immediately knows emptiness, yet does not cling to the knower of emptiness.
Having understood this meaning of the Dharma, they likewise find no self;
since no self can be apprehended, how could there be suffering in this state?
"Emptiness is an unconditioned dharma; its marks, too, cannot be apprehended.
One who can perceive the wisdom of non-self is a true son of the Buddha.

At that time, those hundreds of billions of sentient beings attained the sublime fruit of untainted celestial immortals in their place of birth. They immediately recollected the suffering they had endured in hell during their past lives, and further reflected upon the virtues of the Tathāgata, the Great Man. Knowing how to repay the Buddha’s kindness, they first entered parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, unable to bear the sight of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha entering parinirvāṇa, those sons of the gods who had already attained the fruits spoke in unison with a single voice, reciting this verse:
"We cannot bear to see the Greatly Compassionate One, The Tamer of Men, enter into extinction;
He who can act as a light for all sentient beings— Unable to bear seeing him first pass away, we shall take extinction before him."
Having spoken these words, he entered parinirvāṇa right there.
At that moment, during the kṣaṇa-muhūrta, the World-Honored One vanished from the Brahma palace and arrived between the twin śāla trees.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Today, during the final watch of the night, I shall enter parinirvāṇa; this is my very last sight of sentient beings."

I shall now cause them to rejoice, extinguish all suffering so they may experience happiness, manifest the great supernormal powers of the Tathāgata, and enable those sentient beings to immediately enter the gate of peace and security.
"To manifest the Tathāgata’s nirvana without remainder and to accord with the intentions of all Buddhas, he displays supernatural powers.

At that time, having formed this thought, the World-Honored One lay down on his right side like a lion; with a mind free from fear, he surveyed the entire great assembly of the ten directions like a mighty dragon-elephant.

Having observed thus, he immediately pressed this great earth with the first big toe of his right foot, producing a great sound that caused the six kinds of earthquakes to pervade the worlds of the ten directions, manifesting unimpeded and inconceivable light that illuminated the ten directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted light from all his physical marks.

Having emitted this light, from each and every pore there further issued forth subtle and wondrous rays of light, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; each ray of light universally illumined Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—those lights did not intermingle with one another, nor did they obstruct each other—and in this manner, from the pores, he repeatedly emitted various subtle and wondrous rays of light in succession;
thus, from each and every pore, he again emitted light in succession, returning once more to illuminate everywhere as before.
At that time, the World-Honored One further manifested various supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Having manifested these powers, through the Buddha’s spiritual power and the Buddha’s sustaining power, he caused all sentient beings to become fully endowed with the vision of the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*), such that the realms they perceived were no different from his own.
All those sentient beings dwelling in this buddha-field behold all the buddha-fields illuminated by the light of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Do you see that city in the eastern world-system, one thousand yojanas in circumference and breadth, so vast that its height and depth are likewise the same? Suppose hundreds of thousands of billions of atoms were to fill this city; do you see them?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“So it is, Bhagavān; so it is, Sugata; we have all seen it.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
“What do you think, monks? Is this number of atoms great? The monks replied, “It is so, it is so, Blessed One.”
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"O bhikṣus! If there is anyone who, among all phenomena, can know such unconditioned dharmas as being unborn, unceasing, outflow-free, and unconditioned."
"Those sentient beings who understand in this way shall be liberated from all suffering and all evil realms.
At that time, there were thirty billion sentient beings who, upon hearing this Dharma, immediately attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
Having attained the fruit, they spoke in unison with one voice, reciting this verse:
"The unconditioned dharma is inexhaustible; The outflow-free is likewise imperishable.
Knowing the noble dharma thus, We have realized nirvāṇa."
Knowing that it is attained in this way, he understands the faculties as they truly are;
out of compassion for sentient beings, he reveals the Dharma of causes and conditions.
The Tathāgata has transformed us, pulling out the arrow of poison and the disease.
The All-Knowing One bestows medicine and even Nirvāṇa.
The torch of wisdom now moves swiftly; the eye of wisdom will soon perish.
Pressed by hundreds of millions of sufferings, they emerge from the Saṃjīva Hell.
“The Great Physician who extracts arrows, who heals the diseases of sentient beings,
can save countless multitudes and prevent them from falling into the evil realms.

At that time, the World-Honored One stood upon the bank of the Black Rope Great Hell and emitted a great radiance that shone everywhere throughout that great hell, extracting immeasurable sentient beings from that place and placing them in the heavens.
In the same manner, he likewise delivers all those in the Tapana and Pratāpana hells;

and from the Raurava, Mahāraurava, Saṃghāta, and Mahāsaṃghāta great hells, he extracts immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, establishing them upon the path of wholesome rebirths and the path to nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One again illuminated the eight great hells with golden light.

By the power of this light, all sentient beings whose bodies were touched by it attained peace and happiness; their entire bodies were moistened and benefited, their minds and bodies filled with joy, and their suffering and affliction were eliminated.
Their eyes beheld the ground of the heart with festive joy, attaining refreshing coolness born of compassion, which rendered their bodies secure and tranquil.

Having pervaded the great hells with light, it extinguishes all burning afflictions and flows forth as cool, soft, and moistening moisture. For the sake of bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings within those great hells who are amidst the blazing masses of fire, such light is emitted sequentially from every pore.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with a great radiance, universally covered all immeasurable sentient beings, causing their minds to become supple and fit to be vessels for the Dharma, and endowing them with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits. Then, with subtle and wondrous speech, he spoke these verses:
"I bestow happiness upon the world, Liberating it from all sorrows and sufferings.
Seeing all beings oppressed by suffering, I manifest the path to Nirvana."
The various dharmas I have taught are tranquil, fearless, and blissful;
if one can understand those dharmas, one will not fall into the evil realms.
Those who are able to take refuge in the Buddha will obtain great benefit.
"For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one shall no longer behold any suffering.

At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken these verses, in the space of a kṣaṇa, a lava, and a muhūrta, the assembly of bhikṣus and the multitude of sentient beings became even more numerous than before; furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless Buddhas lying on their right sides upon lion-thrones. Those World-Honored Ones rose from their lion-thrones and once again manifested such supernatural powers.
At that time, the fourfold assembly addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Do all these Buddhas wish to enter parinirvāṇa and manifest supernatural powers within a single kṣaṇa, lava, or muhūrta?"
"What the World-Honored One has manifested now is no different.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "So it is, so it is."

Today, those Buddhas all desire to cast off their final bodies and enter parinirvāṇa. All those Buddhas bear the same name, Śākyamuni; they are all at the site of the Malla clan’s birthplace, beneath the twin śāla trees, reclining upon lion thrones, and shall enter parinirvāṇa during the latter part of this very night.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus throughout the ten directions—namely the south and southwest, the west and northwest, the north and northeast, the east and southeast, as well as the zenith and nadir—saying:
"O bhikṣus! You all!"
"Do you see the immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the eastern direction who have realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The bhikṣus replied, "So it is, so it is, Bhagavān;
we all see them, but we see them by way of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), not by way of ultimate truth (paramārtha)."
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
“Suppose the world-system of the four continents were entirely filled with atoms of dust, extending from the adamantine base up to the Brahma palace. Bhikṣus!”
What do you think? Is there anyone who knows their number?
Is it possible to know their number through an analogy?
The bhikṣus said: “No, World-Honored One!
It would be difficult to know.”
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:

“Suppose, as previously described by way of the analogy of motes of dust, that worlds such as these four-continent systems, and likewise hundreds of thousands of billions of such worlds, were all completely filled with those masses of motes of dust.”

"O Bhikṣus! As for all those atoms—such atoms as these—I see with my physical eye the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, dwelling in this world-system in the eastern direction, as if they were at a distance of a single step. Yet, it is only by means of my physical eye, which is unobstructed and free from discrimination, that I see the worlds before me as previously described;
likewise, it is so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below."

“O Bhikṣus! Suppose there were as many worlds as the four great continents in the universe, filled with hundreds of thousands of billions of those atoms; from the Vajra-limit up to the Brahma-palace, for all the atoms therein, in each and every direction, there are a certain number of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones. In each and every direction, I clearly see all these World-Honored Ones seated at the site of enlightenment—some already seated, some just beginning to sit. All of those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, are identical in name, being called Śākyamuni.
Likewise, there are immeasurable other Buddhas who share the same name as Dīpaṃkara Buddha.”
I further see various Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, whose names are "Victorious Over All" (Sarvavijaya), all sharing the same name;
likewise, there are all these Buddhas named "Lotus Above" (Padmottara); similarly, there are those Buddhas above who share the single name "Renowned Above" (Uttaranāman);
and similarly, there are those Buddhas who share the single name "Krakucchanda."
In this way, I have clearly perceived here all those Buddhas who shared the same name as Konāgamana Buddha;
likewise, those who bore the same name as Kāśyapa Buddha; and likewise, those various Buddhas who each bore the same name.

Each of those Buddhas has their own distinct name; I have attained the most supreme Dharma, the subtle and wondrous Dharma, the ultimate Dharma in this world. Anyone who is able to recite these names shall all obtain roots of goodness.
The individual names of those Buddhas are thus infinite; all such Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, I behold directly from this very place.

All such beings in the present world with their various names—whether they have entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, or are currently dwelling in the world turning the wheel of Dharma—I behold them all directly from this very place.
"Those Buddhas, those World-Honored Ones, appear before me without obstruction or hindrance to my physical eyes.

O Bhikṣus! The Tathāgata possesses such knowledge, and even more excellent than this; he possesses further knowledge that is inconceivable, and further, inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless. Moreover, there are immeasurable and boundless such knowledges and insights."

"O bhikṣus! For this reason, the Tathāgata’s wisdom and vision are boundless; thus they are immeasurable, thus they are incomparable, and thus they are inconceivable. This is so even with the mere fleshly eye, let alone the full extent of the Buddhas' wisdom and Dharma."

“O Bhikṣus! Suppose all sentient beings in this world-system—whether householders or those who have gone forth—were each to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become fully endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.”

Among those World-Honored Ones, there was a son of good family who was able to serve and make offerings with the four requisites for the full duration of an eon, honoring and revering them with various musical instruments and manifold ornaments, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.

Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who can believe this Dharma-gate revealed by me, which displays the teachings of all Buddhas, and who for even a single moment of thought can give rise to the perception of its reality without harboring doubt, then the merit they obtain at the very moment of generating that resolve will approximate the merit of all Tathāgatas. Moreover, it surpasses the great amount of merit gained by all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm who, having realized the omniscience of all Buddhas, were to make offerings for an entire kalpa; the merit of those who generate a single thought of faith in this Dharma-gate is greater than that.
"If there are bodhisattvas who have faith in this wisdom, those bodhisattvas shall draw near to the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all the World-Honored Ones.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was speaking of these merits of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), sixty-two billion sentient beings who had turned their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* again gave rise to regressive thoughts.

Why is this? Because the Buddha’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is difficult to realize, we have merely attained the fruit of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-phala*) by extinguishing all suffering right here;
furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who remain on the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, ten nayutas of bodhisattvas accomplished the initial arousal of the mind toward enlightenment;
additionally, thirty-two billion bodhisattvas and others attained the dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, filled with grief and anguish, his face drenched in tears, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason did I wish for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha to enter parinirvāṇa so soon?"
He has caused immeasurable and boundless multitudes of beings to emerge from my realm.
Now, World-Honored One!

During the brief interval before the sun appears in the east when it is still dark yellow, the Buddha-work you have performed is as if you had remained for an entire kalpa; yet even if you were to remain for an entire kalpa, you could not surpass this in benefiting and delivering such a multitude of sentient beings.
"What is called abiding in the path to parinirvāṇa causes the realm of the Tathāgata now to become entirely empty.
When Māra Pāpīyas had spoken these words, the Buddha said to Pāpīyas: "Do not weep, Pāpīyas!"
"You still have many who do not perform wholesome deeds and lack faith; they are your friends within your domain, and you are their companion.
At that time, the World-Honored One took some dust from the ground with his fingernail and addressed Māra Pāpīyas: "What do you think?"
"Is the dust on my fingernails more,
or is the dust upon this great earth more?
When he had spoken these words, Māra Pāpīyān addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The dust upon a fingernail is so slight as to be beyond description.
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed Pāpīyas:
“Pāpīyan, it is like the dust on a fingernail, which is extremely small; those sentient beings whom I have delivered and led into nirvāṇa are even fewer than that dust on a fingernail.”

For example, the dust particles of the great earth are exceedingly numerous, immeasurable and boundless; likewise, the sentient beings within your realm are also exceedingly numerous and immeasurable.
Pāpīyān! Do not grieve; you should instead give rise to joy. Why is this?
"Pāpīyan, it is because there are many beings within your realm who possess great earth and soil.
However, these beings have themselves committed unwholesome deeds and are far from nirvāṇa; this is not your doing."
Why is this? Because, Pāpīyan,
the realm of sentient beings has no limit.
"Whatever you wish to do, do it now; this very day, in the latter part of the night, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"O bhikṣus! You bhikṣus!"
“Have you seen the Buddhas of this world?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!”
"So it is, so it is, Bhagavān; we have indeed seen them.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"These buddha-fields are further immeasurable in number. You should know: have you all seen the adornments of these buddha-fields?"
"Furthermore, have you seen how the various bodhisattvas adorn their pure lands?
And furthermore, have you seen how the various śrāvakas adorn [their realms]?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
So it is, Bhagavān; so it is, Sugata.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
“The Tathāgata knows and sees in this way; moreover, he knows and sees immeasurably more than the number mentioned above, and he fully understands even further immeasurable things. Monks!
Even if I were to speak for an eon regarding such matters as the adornments of these buddha-fields, just as I have seen them in the worlds of the ten directions, it would still be the same;
even if I were to speak with further doubled metaphors and detailed explanations for a hundred eons, a thousand eons, billions of eons, or nayutas of eons, they could not be fully exhausted.
"However, O bhikṣus!

That which was to be done by the Teacher has been completed for the sake of the śrāvakas; in all respects, I have finished my teaching, having fully revealed all internal and external phenomena and manifested the true mind."
The Buddhas have no stinginess regarding the Dharma and there is nothing they cannot explain, even down to a single blade of grass or as much as a single hair. You, bhikṣus!
From this day forward, you must practice diligently in accordance with the Dharma.

I have manifested nirvāṇa for you; I have taught you the path to nirvāṇa; and I have brought the roots of goodness of sentient beings to fulfillment. The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment that I have realized was attained through the great ascetic practices and hardships I underwent in the past.
"You all must now fully receive and uphold that Great Dharma so that it does not disappear.
You should practice in this manner.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested great supernormal powers, such that all sentient beings in this world-system were able to hear and know all the teachings and the places where they were taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
All the instructions of those Tathāgatas, and all sentient beings who have received and followed those instructions, have already realized and known them;
furthermore, there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who abide in the three types of knowledge;
and there are ten billion hundred thousand sentient beings who have resolved their minds on Bodhi and abide in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, there were ten hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* beings who dwelt in the stage of *pratyekabuddha*;
the remaining beings attained the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
In this manner, immeasurable, boundless, *asaṃkhyeya*, incalculable, unfathomable, and inconceivable *nayuta* numbers of beings, having heard this Dharma, obtained great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus,
you should know that I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa."
"You all! You should uphold the Tathāgata’s teaching for the sake of your own benefit and for the benefit of others. You, O bhikṣus!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, along with the devas, humans, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, and all other beings in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, received it upon their heads and practiced accordingly.
The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Four Youthful Disciples, Scroll II.
